		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Supertex, Inc. (&#x201C;Supertex,&#x201D; the &#x201C;Company,&#x201D; &#x201C;we,&#x201D; and &#x201C;us&#x201D;) is a producer of high voltage analog and mixed signal semiconductor components.&nbsp;&nbsp;We design, develop, manufacture, and market integrated circuits (&#x201C;ICs&#x201D;), utilizing state-of-the-art high voltage DMOS, HVCMOS and HVBiCMOS analog and mixed signal technologies.&nbsp;&nbsp;With respect to our DMOS transistor products, we maintain an established </font><font style="display: inline;">application specific </font><font style="display: inline;">position in providing key products for the industrial, telecommunication</font><font style="display: inline;">s</font><font style="display: inline;">, instrumentation, medical, and automatic test equipment (&#x201C;ATE&#x201D;) industries.&nbsp;&nbsp;We are also an industry leader in high voltage </font><font style="display: inline;">ICs</font><font style="display: inline;"> (HVCMOS and HVBiCMOS), taking advantage of the best features of CMOS, bipolar and DMOS technologies and integrating them into </font><font style="display: inline;">a single</font><font style="display: inline;"> chip.&nbsp;&nbsp;These ICs are used in the medical ultrasound imaging, </font><font style="display: inline;">LED </font><font style="display: inline;">backlighting</font><font style="display: inline;"> for monitors and LCD TVs</font><font style="display: inline;">, LED general lighting, telecommunications, printer, flat panel display, industrial and consumer </font><font style="display: inline;">product </font><font style="display: inline;">industries.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">We market and sell our products through direct sales personnel, independent sales representatives and distributors in the United States of America and abroad, primarily to original equipment manufacturers of electronic products. </font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">Our executive offices are located at 1235 Bordeaux Drive, Sunnyvale, California, 94089, and our principal manufacturing facilities are located in San Jose, California, and in Hong Kong. We have two design centers, one in our Sunnyvale worldwide headquarters and the other in our wholly owned subsidiary, Supertex, Ltd</font><font style="display: inline;">.</font><font style="display: inline;"> in Hong Kong.&nbsp;&nbsp;Our Hong Kong facility also houses the headquarters of Supertex, Ltd., worldwide logistic and distribution center, and production test facilities. We </font><font style="display: inline;">maintain ten direct</font><font style="display: inline;"> field sales offices located in the following areas: </font><font style="display: inline;">Arlington</font><font style="display: inline;">, Texas; Oley, Pennsylvania; the United Kingdom; Germany; Hong Kong, Shanghai &amp; Shenzhen, China; Taiwan; Japan; and South Korea.&nbsp;&nbsp;Our headquarters&#x2019; mailing address is 1235 Bordeaux Drive, Sunnyvale, California 94089 and the telephone number is (408) 222-8888.&nbsp;&nbsp;Our website address is </font><font style="display: inline;">www.supertex.com</font><font style="display: inline;">. The content of the website is not incorporated into this Form 10-K.</font>
		</p>

			<font style="display: inline;font-weight:normal;">Our four target markets for our semiconductor components are medical electronics, lighting </font><font style="display: inline;font-weight:normal;">and backlighting </font><font style="display: inline;font-weight:normal;">using </font>

		</p>

</div>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-weight:bold;font-family:Times New Roman;;font-size: 11pt"><font style="display: inline;font-weight:normal;">light emitting diodes (&#x201C;LEDs&#x201D;), printers and devices using electro-luminescent (&#x201C;EL&#x201D;) lamps, and telecommunication. Our products are primarily used in medical ultrasound imaging equipment; LED modules for general lighting and for backlighting LCD TVs and computer monitors; large commercial ink-jet printers and EL modules for backlighting cellphone keypads and other LCD displays; and optical </font><font style="display: inline;font-weight:normal;">micro-electro-mechanical systems ("</font><font style="display: inline;font-weight:normal;">MEMS") for</font><font style="display: inline;font-weight:normal;"> telecommunications switches.&nbsp;&nbsp;Our products are basically interface products, interfacing between low voltage logic circuits and high voltage &#x201C;real world&#x201D; media and vice versa.&nbsp;&nbsp;We supply both standard and custom products. The typical gestation period of our new products from introduction through design-in by the customer to volume production is one year, although certain products for medical applications have longer gestation periods. During fiscal 2013, we introduced twenty-two new standard products, the majority of which were aimed at high growth markets such as medical ultrasound imaging and solid-state LED lighting.&nbsp; </font><font style="display: inline;font-weight:normal;">We expect our recently introduced devices as well as our future new devices to be drivers for increased revenue as our customers introduce and start volume production of their products containing our devices after designing our devices into their products under development, conducting successful product qualification tests, and obtaining their end customer acceptance.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-weight:bold;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-weight:normal;">We also provide custom processing services for the manufacture of ICs, using customer-owned designs and mask tooling. Under this &#x201C;custom processing service&#x201D; or &#x201C;foundry&#x201D; arrangement, a tangible product is made and sold, and the Company bears the risk of loss until title is passed</font><font style="display: inline;font-weight:normal;"> on to the customer</font><font style="display: inline;font-weight:normal;"> at the time of shipment from our facility. During fiscal 2013, sales of custom processed products represented approximately 14% of our total revenues compared to 12%</font><font style="display: inline;font-weight:normal;"> and 11%</font><font style="display: inline;font-weight:normal;"> in fiscal 2012</font><font style="display: inline;font-weight:normal;"> and 2011, respectively</font><font style="display: inline;font-weight:normal;">. &nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;font-weight:normal;">Sales of custom processing services are </font><font style="display: inline;font-weight:normal;">not reported separately but are</font><font style="display: inline;font-weight:normal;"> included </font><font style="display: inline;font-weight:normal;">with</font><font style="display: inline;font-weight:normal;">in the</font><font style="display: inline;font-weight:normal;">ir respective</font><font style="display: inline;font-weight:normal;"> target markets.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">The products in our </font><font style="display: inline;">four </font><font style="display: inline;">target markets are described below.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;">The </font><font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;">Medical Electronics Market</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">We have provided both standard and high-end custom ICs to the ultrasound imaging market for many years and have established key business relationships with leading OEMs.&nbsp;&nbsp;The products we manufacture for this market include high voltage analog multiplexer switches, pulsers, beam formers, transmit/receive (T/R) switches, low noise amplifiers (&#x201C;LNA&#x201D;), high-speed MOSFET drivers and discrete high voltage MOSFETs and arrays. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">We are the leading high voltage analog switch</font><font style="display: inline;">/multiplexor</font><font style="display: inline;"> and high voltage integrated pulser product provider in this market segment.&nbsp;&nbsp;In recent years, the overall ultrasound market has been shifting to portable ultrasound imaging units. These high-performance, portable, and affordable medical imaging systems are accelerating the proliferation to other applications in addition to existing cardiology and obstetrics/gynecology applications. Even within these traditional clinical diagnostic segments, cardiology ultrasound imaging is showing an exciting pipeline of technological </font><font style="display: inline;">innovations and strong </font><font style="display: inline;">volume growth. The adoption of ultrasound imaging by new user groups</font><font style="display: inline;">, &nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;"> surgeons and emergency ward physicians</font><font style="display: inline;">,</font><font style="display: inline;"> is also spurring medical ultrasound imaging system market growth.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Our high voltage expertise affords us a leading position in the ultrasound &#x201C;transmit&#x201D; market with MOSFET drivers, high voltage analog switches and multiplexers, high voltage pulsers, and complementary high voltage MOSFET arrays. However, at the request of certain customers, we have designed a low cost, high performance LNA which is </font><font style="display: inline;">targeted for portable ultrasound systems due to its low power consumption and high performance.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">We released eight new medical ultrasound products in fiscal 2013, and expect to introduce a greater number of products for the ultrasound imaging market in fiscal 2014 even though they are increasingly more complex.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">We believe that the ultrasound imaging market into which we sell our products continues to have long-term growth prospects. </font><font style="display: inline;">The capabilities and performance of the machines that utilize our products continue to improve, allowing them to be used more broadly across a wider spectrum of imaging applications than ever before. Geographically</font><font style="display: inline;">, the market is expanding as well. Traditionally, the United States, Europe and Japan have been the main designers and producers of medical ultrasound machines. While companies in these areas continue to grow and develop new </font>
		</p>

			<font style="display: inline;">Many of our </font><font style="display: inline;">IC</font><font style="display: inline;">s used in medical ultrasound systems are also being designed into non-destructive testing (&#x201C;NDT&#x201D;) applications, which is a relatively new and growing market.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;">The LED Drivers Market</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">We offer</font><font style="display: inline;"> an extensive line of high-performance LED driver products for the solid-state</font><font style="display: inline;"> lighting and back</font><font style="display: inline;">lighting market, ranging from simple, low-cost linear regulators to feature-rich switching regulators configured in buck, boost, buck-boost, and single ended primary inductance converter (&#x201C;SEPIC&#x201D;) topologies. As one of the pioneers in the high voltage LED driver IC market, we have established a strong market position.&nbsp;&nbsp;We have developed many efficient and cost effective products for general lighting in </font><font style="display: inline;">infrastructure, </font><font style="display: inline;">automotive, industrial, and consumer applications, and for backlighting LCD TVs and computer monitors. Our LED drivers can be used in 3D TVs as well. We expect to introduce a significant number of</font><font style="display: inline;"> new LED driver products </font><font style="display: inline;">for the solid-state lighting market in fiscal 2014</font><font style="display: inline;"> and we expect this market will continue to increase</font><font style="display: inline;">.</font>
		</p>

We are one of the key providers of EL drivers for cell phones and watches, and we have a significant share of this market due to our patented inductorless EL driver ICs.&nbsp;&nbsp;EL is preferred over LED when space, power consumption and uniformity of the display are important</font><font style="display: inline;"> features</font><font style="display: inline;">. &nbsp;</font></p></td></tr></table></div>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;">The </font><font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;">Telecommunications (&#x201C;Telecom&#x201D;) Market</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">We provide high voltage amplifier ICs to drive optical MEMS for the telecommunications market for use in optical switching applications. Our MEMS driver ICs feature high channel count per chip and are capable of driving output voltages of up to 300 volts.&nbsp;&nbsp;We also produce high voltage electronic switch ICs that replace typical electromechanical hook switches in telephones, high voltage ICs for use as ring generators, and protection ICs for line cards. </font>

		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;;font-size: 11pt"><font style="display: inline;">In the DMOS transistor technology, we focus on certain specific niches such as very low threshold, low capacitance, and low leakage devices where these features justify a premium and are most suitable for special applications such as medical ultrasound imaging, LED lighting</font><font style="display: inline;"> and backlighting</font><font style="display: inline;">, telecommunication, ATE, and hand-held instruments.&nbsp;&nbsp;These high voltage DMOS transistor products also serve as building blocks and predecessors to a fully integrated solution -- our high voltage ICs.</font>

			<font style="display: inline;">We operate in one business segment.&nbsp;&nbsp;Information regarding Supertex, Inc.&#x2019;s Segment Reporting can be found in </font><font style="display: inline;">Note 13 to the</font><font style="display: inline;"> Consolidated Financial Statements.</font>

		<p style="margin:0pt;font-weight:bold;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Research and Development</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">We incurred expenses of $13,976,000, $14,399,000 and $14,851,000 on research and development activities during fiscal years 2013, 2012 and 2011, respectively. Our research and development activities in fiscal 2013 were dedicated to developing new high voltage processes, both internal and with external foundry partners, resulting in a total of twenty-two new standard product introductions. The products introduced in fiscal 2013 were primarily targeted for use in the rapidly growing LED and medical ultrasound industries, although we are also developing new standard products for the printer/EL driver, telecom, and industrial/other markets as well as&nbsp;&nbsp;some custom products for specific customer applications. As we move forward into fiscal 2014, we expect to continue to leverage our newly-developed high voltage designs and processes to introduce many more new products for these markets, as well as for our other target markets. Currently, there are approximately 50 products in development, many of which are expected to be completed during fiscal years 2014 and 2015, although there is no assurance that all these products will be completed or launched due to market conditions, technical difficulties, or other factors.</font><font style="display: inline;font-weight:bold;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Our products, which we strive to make best in class, have experienced very good traction in the marketplace, leading to significant design wins in all our target markets. We believe best in class products are those that provide the best performance at a competitive price, where in the case of LED drivers performance is measured by receiving high input voltage and producing tightly controlled output current. Most of our design wins resulted from close collaboration with the Tier-1 customers in their respective markets and a shorter design and development cycle to support our customers&#x2019; needs. We believe that our position as a leading supplier in our targeted markets can only be maintained through continuous investments in research and development. We focus our efforts on designing new products with existing process technologies while also developing new process technologies to be used for future products. We continuously strive to effectively monitor and control our research and development programs in order to obtain improved performance and greater technological achievements at lower costs. Because we have our own wafer fabrication facility (&#x201C;fab&#x201D;) with ample capacity and our designers have years of experience in our target markets, we can tailor our processes and circuits to meet customer </font><font style="display: inline;">needs which we can respond to much more expediently and ramp up production. For </font><font style="display: inline;">deep submicron</font><font style="display: inline;"> sizes, we u</font><font style="display: inline;">se our foundry partners in Asia. We have developed many new products to reduce cost with these foundry partners.&nbsp; </font>

Sales through our distributors are evidenced by a binding purchase order on a transaction-by-transaction basis.&nbsp;&nbsp;Because of the uncertainty associated with pricing concessions and possible returns, with the exception of certain products, we defer the recognition of such sales and the related costs of sales until our distributors have sold the merchandise to their end customers.&nbsp;&nbsp;Our distributors provide us an inventory balance report at the end of each period, which allows us to determine products sold to their end customers.</font><font style="display: inline;"> Notwithstanding the timing of their sales of our products, our distributors are obligated to pay us according to our regular payment terms.</font>

		<p style="margin:0pt;font-weight:bold;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Competition</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">In general, competition among suppliers of semiconductor components is intense, especially in the analog sector where the gross margins are traditionally much higher, including products for the medical electronics, imaging, telecom, LED lighting, and industrial/other markets we primarily serve.&nbsp;&nbsp;In general, we face different competitors in different markets or for different products. We compete with several larger analog semiconductor companies with far greater resources although we believe we have defended our market-leading positions successfully for many years. For example, we compete with Maxim, Hitachi and Texas Instruments in the medical electronics market; we compete with Rogers Durel and Micrel in the EL market; and we compete with Texas Instruments, Cirrus Logic, Power Integrations, NXP, O2 Micro, and other Asian suppliers in the LED lighting and backlighting market. In addition, we may compete with some of our own customers which have in-house semiconductor design capabilities and may develop and in-source products to replace those that we currently sell them as did Samsung in fiscal 2011 for our LED drivers for backlighting their LED TVs. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Our products are generally not sold pursuant to long term contracts, enabling our customers to switch suppliers if they choose, making us more vulnerable to competitors. Competition in the industry is based primarily upon factors such as product prices, product performance, product line diversity, delivery capabilities, customer relationships and the ability to adapt to rapid technological change in the development of new and improved products.&nbsp;&nbsp;The weighing of these factors varies depending on the specific needs of a customer at any given point in time. We believe we are competitive with respect to these factors. However, market statistics are not generally available for many of our products. Many of our domestic and foreign competitors have larger facilities, more financial, technical, and human resources, and more diverse product lines.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Among our competitive advantages and core competencies are the following: (1) high voltage analog and mixed signal circuit design and device intellectual property; (2) high voltage DMOS, HVCMOS and HVBiCMOS wafer fabrication (&#x201C;fab&#x201D;) processes that are high yielding and low cost and do not require our fab to have the latest submicron feature sizes; (3) owning and operating our own fab to protect our IP; and (4) having long-term close working relationships with our key customers.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;We capitalize on our leadership position in the niche markets we focus on by working very closely with our customers to help them with next generation products, thereby achieving design-wins in order to maintain or grow market-share in our target markets. We compete primarily on the basis of product innovation and responsiveness to changing needs of customers, including both product specifications and delivery requirements. In short, we strive to be the technology enablers for our customers.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-weight:bold;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Patents and Licenses</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">We hold </font><font style="display: inline;">forty-seven</font><font style="display: inline;"> United States patents which will expire between </font><font style="display: inline;">2015 and 2031</font><font style="display: inline;">, an</font><font style="display: inline;">d we have</font><font style="display: inline;"> additional United States patent applications pending. Although we believe that our patents may have value, there can be no assurance that our current patents or any additional patents that we may obtain in the future will provide meaningful protection from competition.&nbsp;&nbsp;We believe that our success depends primarily on the experience, creative skills, technical expertise, and marketing ability of our personnel rather than on the ownership of patents.&nbsp;&nbsp;Patents may, however, be useful for cross-license purposes and have served us well in the past.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">We are not aware of any of our products infringing on any valid patent or other proprietary rights of third parties but we cannot be certain that they do not.&nbsp;&nbsp;If infringement would be alleged, there is no assurance that the necessary licenses could be obtained, or if obtained, would be on terms or conditions that would not have a material adverse effect on the Company.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-weight:bold;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Employees</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">As of </font><font style="display: inline;">March 30, 2013</font><font style="display: inline;">, we had </font><font style="display: inline;">330</font><font style="display: inline;"> full time employees primarily located in Northern California and Hong Kong.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>

			<font style="text-indent:0pt;margin-left:0pt; width:193.5pt;"></font><font style="text-indent:0pt;margin-left:0pt; width:-1pt;text-align:left"><font style="display: inline;font-weight:bold;"></font><font style="display: inline;font-weight:bold;"></font></font>

		</p>

</div>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;;font-size: 11pt"><font style="display: inline;">Many of our employees are highly skilled, an</font><font style="display: inline;">d we believe our continued growth and success will depend in part on our ability to attract and retain such employees.&nbsp;&nbsp;At times, like other semiconductor manufacturers, we experience difficulty in hiring and retaining sufficient numbers of skilled personnel, especially experienced analog integrated circuit designers.&nbsp;&nbsp;Engineers with analog circuit experience and training are scarcer than experienced digital engineers.&nbsp;&nbsp;Analog and mix</font><font style="display: inline;">ed</font><font style="display: inline;">-signal expertise tends to be learned over time based on experience and on-the-job-training, whereas digital expertise </font><font style="display: inline;">is relatively easier to learn and </font><font style="display: inline;">is extensively taught in universities due to its overall market size.&nbsp;&nbsp;Engineers with high voltage analog circuit experience are even scarcer.&nbsp;&nbsp;We often recruit top college graduates directly from universities and train them ourselves.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">We believe that the compensation, benefits, and incentives offered to our employees are competitive with those generally offered throughout the semiconductor industry.&nbsp;&nbsp;There are no collective bargaining agreements between our employees and us, and there has been no work stoppage due to labor difficulties.&nbsp;&nbsp;We consider our employee relations to be good.</font>

			<font style="display: inline;">Item 1A.&nbsp; </font><font style="display: inline;">Risk Factors</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">The following are certain risk factors that could affect our business, financial results and results of operations.&nbsp;&nbsp;These risk factors should be considered in connection with evaluating the forward-looking statements contained in this Annual Report on Form 10-K because these factors could cause the actual results and conditions to differ materially from those projected in the forward-looking statements.&nbsp;&nbsp;Investing in our common stock involves risks, including those described below.&nbsp;&nbsp;These risks are not the only ones that we face.&nbsp;&nbsp;If any of the risks actually occur, our business, financial condition or results of operations could be negatively affected.&nbsp;&nbsp;In that case, the trading price of our common stock could decline</font><font style="display: inline;"> materially and you could lose a corresponding portion of your investment, although we believe a substantial portion of our current stock price is based upon our cash position.</font>
		</p>

			<font style="display: inline;">As required by Section 1502 of the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act of 2010 on August 22, 2012, the SEC promulgated new disclosure requirements for manufacturers of products containing certain minerals which are mined from the Democratic Republic of Congo and adjoining countries. These &#x201C;conflict minerals&#x201D; are commonly found in metals used in the manufacture of semiconductors. Manufacturers are also required to disclose their efforts to prevent the sourcing of such minerals and metals produced from them. The new disclosure rules take effect for calendar 2013 and require that we file our first report on or before May 31, 2014 and will require us to undertake additional supply chain due diligence to comply. The implementation of these new regulations may involve a material expense on our part </font><font style="display: inline;">and may limit the sourcing and availability of some of the metals used in the manufacture of our products. The regulations may also reduce the number of suppliers who provide conflict-free metals, and may affect our ability to obtain products in sufficient quantities or at competitive prices. </font><font style="display: inline;">Also</font><font style="display: inline;">, some of our customers may elect to disqualify us as a supplier if we are unable to verify that the metals used in our products free of conflict minerals</font><font style="display: inline;">.</font></p></td></tr></table></div>

The U.S. Department of State closed the case without fine and without taking further action, while reserving the right to re-open the case if the circumstances warrant, and</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">cautioned us to take actions to strengthen our compliance processes and procedures, which we&nbsp;believe we have done.</font></p></td></tr></table></div>

			<font style="text-indent:0pt;margin-left:0pt; width:193.5pt;"></font><font style="text-indent:0pt;margin-left:0pt; width:-1pt;text-align:left"><font style="display: inline;font-weight:bold;"></font><font style="display: inline;font-weight:bold;"></font></font>

			<font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">We have had share repurchase programs in place since 1992 under which our board of directors authorized us to repurchase an aggregate of </font><font style="display: inline;">4,844</font><font style="display: inline;">,</font><font style="display: inline;">145</font><font style="display: inline;"> shares. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Since the inception of these repurchase programs in 1992 through </font><font style="display: inline;">March 30, 2013</font><font style="display: inline;">, we have repurchased a total of </font><font style="display: inline;">4,015,983</font><font style="display: inline;"> shares of the common stock </font><font style="display: inline;">for an aggregate cost of approximate</font><font style="display: inline;">ly </font><font style="display: inline;">$68,630,000</font><font style="display: inline;">. Upo</font><font style="display: inline;">n their repurchase, shares are restored to the status of authorized but unissued shares. As of </font><font style="display: inline;">March 30, 2013</font><font style="display: inline;">, &nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">there were 828,162 </font><font style="display: inline;">shares authorized for </font><font style="display: inline;">future </font><font style="display: inline;">repurchase under our current program</font><font style="display: inline;">.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">In January, 2011, our board of directors designated $60 million of our cash, cash equivalents, and investments for a major stock repurchase under our share repurchase programs through the end of fiscal 2013, of which we ended up using approximately $32 million.&nbsp;&nbsp;Management currently determines whether to repurchase some or all of the remaining 828,162 shares under our current share repurchase program based on factors such as the price of our stock, the dollar volume of transactions in our stock, and whether we learn of material non-public information at a time when we do not have a 10b5-1 program in place which permits us to continue buying shares in the market.</font>
		</p>

			<font style="display: inline;font-weight:bold;">Item 7.&nbsp;&nbsp;Management's Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-weight:bold;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Overview</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 6pt;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">We design, develop, manufacture, and market integrated circuits (&#x201C;ICs&#x201D;) and application specific discrete DMOS transistors, utilizing state-of-the-art high voltage DMOS, HVCMOS and HVBiCMOS analog and mixed signal technologies.&nbsp;&nbsp;We are an industry leader in certain high voltage ICs (HVCMOS and HVBiCMOS) which take advantage of the best features of CMOS, bipolar and DMOS technologies and integrate them into </font><font style="display: inline;">a single</font><font style="display: inline;"> IC.&nbsp;&nbsp;These ICs are used for medical ultrasound imaging, LED backlighting for LCD TVs and computer monitors, LED general lighting, telecommunications, printer, flat panel display, industrial and consumer product industries. We also offer custom design and production of application specific ICs as well as custom processing services using customer-owned designs and mask tooling with our process technologies. Our current growth strategy relies on our ability to continuously and successfully introduce and market new innovative products that meet our customers&#x2019; requirements.</font>

		<p style="margin:0pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-weight:bold;">Critical Accounting Policies and Estimates</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Our discussion and analysis of financial condition and results of operations are based upon our Consolidated Financial Statements, which have been prepared in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America. Note 1 to the Consolidated Financial Statements describes the significant accounting policies and methods used in the preparation of the Consolidated Financial Statements. The preparation of these financial statements requires us to make estimates and judgments that affect the reported amounts of assets, liabilities, revenues and expenses.&nbsp; </font><font style="display: inline;">Significant estimates in these financial statements include revenue recognition, </font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">net realizable value of inventories</font><font style="display: inline;">, &nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">provision for income taxes and tax valuation allowance</font><font style="display: inline;">,</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">and </font><font style="display: inline;">asset impairments. </font><font style="display: inline;">We base our estimates on historical experience and on various other assumptions that are believed to be reasonable under the circumstances, the results of which form the basis for making judgments about the carrying values of assets and liabilities that are not readily apparent from other sources.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">We consider the accounting policies described below to be our critical accounting policies. Our critical accounting policies are those that both (1) are most important to the portrayal of the financial condition and results of </font>
		</p>

			&nbsp;

		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;;font-size: 11pt"><font style="display: inline;">operations and (2) require management&#x2019;s most difficult, subjective, or complex judgments, often requiring estimates about matters that are inherently uncertain. These critical accounting policies reflect our significant judgments, assumptions, and estimates used in the preparation of the Consolidated Financial Statements. Our management has discussed the development and selection of these critical accounting policies and estimates with the audit committee of our board of directors and the audit committee has reviewed our disclosures in relation to this report.</font>

		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;">Revenue Recognition</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">We recognize </font><font style="display: inline;">revenue from direct product sales to end-user customers upon transfer of title and risk of loss, which is upon shipment of the product provided persuasive evidence of an arrangement exists, the price is fixed or determinable, no significant obligations remain, and collection of the resulting receivable is reasonably assured.&nbsp;&nbsp;For sales to OEMs, we use either a binding purchase order or signed agreement as evidence of an arrangement.&nbsp;&nbsp;For those customers wh</font><font style="display: inline;">o</font><font style="display: inline;"> have a hub arrangement, we recognize revenue when our products are transferred from the hub to the customer&#x2019;s manufacturing facility or to its assembly subcontractor&#x2019;s manufacturing facility. Sales through our distributors are evidenced by binding purchase orders on a transaction-by-transaction basis.&nbsp;&nbsp;Because of the uncertainty associated with pricing concessions and possible returns, with the exception of certain </font><font style="display: inline;">non-returnable </font><font style="display: inline;">products, we defer the recognition of revenue to all our distributors, domestic and foreign, and the related costs of sales until our distributors have sold the merchandise to their end customers.&nbsp; </font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">We also provide custom processing services </font><font style="display: inline;">for ICs in our fab </font><font style="display: inline;">using customer-owned designs and mask tooling.&nbsp;&nbsp;Under this &#x201C;custom processing service&#x201D; arrangement, a tangible product is sold, and we bear the risk of loss until title is passed</font><font style="display: inline;"> on to the customer at the time of shipment</font><font style="display: inline;">.&nbsp;&nbsp;Title to the product under the &#x201C;custom processing service&#x201D; arrangement is passed to the customer at the time of shipment.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">From time to time, deferred revenue results from up-front billings </font><font style="display: inline;">to</font><font style="display: inline;"> customers under non-recurring engineering (&#x201C;NRE&#x201D;) contracts. </font><font style="display: inline;">We recognize revenue from our</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">NRE </font><font style="display: inline;">contracts upon completion of contract milestones, which corresponds to when we provide the services and/or products.&nbsp;&nbsp;Revenue is deferred for any amounts received prior to completion of contract milestones</font><font style="display: inline;">,</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">as provided for under current accounting guidance</font><font style="display: inline;">. Some of our NRE contracts include formal customer acceptance provisions</font><font style="display: inline;"> in which </font><font style="display: inline;">case, at the end of each period, we determine whether customer acceptance has been obtained for the specific milestone.&nbsp;&nbsp;If customer acceptance has not been obtained, we defer the recognition of such revenue until customer acceptance is obtained.</font><font style="display: inline;"> To date, revenue from NRE contracts has represented an insignificant portion of our total revenue.</font><font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;">Inventory Valuation</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Our i</font><font style="display: inline;">nventories are stated at the lower of cost (determined on a first-in, first-out basis) or net realizable value</font><font style="display: inline;">. They are </font><font style="display: inline;">high technology p</font><font style="display: inline;">roducts which</font><font style="display: inline;"> are specialized in nature and subject to rapid technological obsolescence.&nbsp;&nbsp;Standard manufacturing cost includes materials, labor, and overhead costs including depreciation, and includes factors for estimated production yield and throughput time.&nbsp;&nbsp;We determine net realizable value of our inventories based on the last selling price, net of selling cost, of our products prior to the balance sheet date.&nbsp;&nbsp;If there has been no recent sale of a particular product, the expected selling price, net of selling cost is deemed as the net realizable value.&nbsp;&nbsp;I</font><font style="display: inline;">nventory balances are adjusted to approximate the lower of our standard manufacturing cost or net realizable value.</font><font style="display: inline;"> Any adjustment to write down inventory to net realizable value is charged to cost of sales in the period that the adjustment is made.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Additionally, we </font><font style="display: inline;">evaluate our ending inventories for excess quantities and obsolescence at each balance sheet date. This evaluation includes analyses of sales levels by product and projections of future demand during the </font><font style="display: inline;">next 12 months, which may involve a great deal of management judgment.&nbsp;&nbsp;Inventories on hand in excess of forecasted demand and inventories that we consider obsolete are written down. We make judgments in establishing inventory net book value and do not write down inventory if management believes certain excess or obsolete inventory will be sold within 12 months. In addition, we age our inventory based on start date.&nbsp;&nbsp;Inventory that has been inactive for more than one year is considered slow moving inventory and is a</font><font style="display: inline;">utomatically</font><font style="display: inline;"> written down and charged to cost </font>
		</p>

		</p>

			&nbsp;

		</p>

			<font style="display: inline;font-weight:bold;font-size:10pt;"> &nbsp; &nbsp;</font>

			&nbsp;

			<font style="text-indent:0pt;margin-left:0pt; width:193.5pt;"></font><font style="text-indent:0pt;margin-left:0pt; width:-1pt;text-align:left"><font style="display: inline;font-weight:bold;"></font><font style="display: inline;font-weight:bold;"></font></font>

		</p>

</div>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;;font-size: 11pt"><font style="display: inline;">of sales</font><font style="display: inline;">, unless overridden by management</font><font style="display: inline;">. Subsequent changes in facts and circumstances do not result in the reduction of the allowance until these inventories are subsequently sold or scrapped.&nbsp;&nbsp;Any proceeds received will favorably affect gross margin</font><font style="display: inline;"> for the period</font><font style="display: inline;">.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">While we have programs</font><font style="display: inline;"> whose objective is</font><font style="display: inline;"> to minimize the required inventories on hand </font><font style="display: inline;">according to the field sales forecasts </font><font style="display: inline;">and </font><font style="display: inline;">we </font><font style="display: inline;">consider technological obsolescence when adjusting inventory carrying values to market values, it is possible that </font><font style="display: inline;">future demand or market conditions </font><font style="display: inline;">could be</font><font style="display: inline;"> less favorable than our projections, </font><font style="display: inline;">in which case </font><font style="display: inline;">additional inventory write-downs may be required and will be reflected in cost of sales in the period the revision is made.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;">Accounting for Income Taxes</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Income taxes are accounted for under the asset and liability method. We make certain estimates and judgments in determining income tax expense for financial statement purposes. These estimates and judgments occur in the calculation of certain deferred tax assets and liabilities, which arise from timing differences in the recognition of revenue and expense for tax and financial statement purposes. Such deferred income tax assets and liabilities are recognized for the future tax consequences attributable to differences between the financial statement carrying amounts of existing assets and liabilities and their respective tax base, operating losses and tax credit carry-forwards. Changes in tax rates affect the deferred income tax assets and liabilities and are recognized in the period in which the tax rates are enacted. </font><br /><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp; &nbsp;</font><br /><font style="display: inline;">Our management must determine the probability that </font><font style="display: inline;">we</font><font style="display: inline;"> will be able to utilize </font><font style="display: inline;">our</font><font style="display: inline;"> deferred tax assets. If we determine that recovery is unlikely, then a valuation allowance against </font><font style="display: inline;">our</font><font style="display: inline;"> deferred tax asset must be recorded by increasing income tax expense. As of </font><font style="display: inline;">March 30, 2013</font><font style="display: inline;">, we believe that our deferred tax assets recorded on our balance sheet will be utilized</font><font style="display: inline;">. &nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">However, should there be a change in our ability to utilize or recover our deferred tax assets, an additional income tax expense would be incurred in the period in which it was determined that the recovery is not probable.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">On February 20, 2009, California </font><font style="display: inline;">enacted</font><font style="display: inline;"> tax-related economic incentives and tax increases</font><font style="display: inline;"> which </font><font style="display: inline;">includ</font><font style="display: inline;">ed</font><font style="display: inline;"> an election to apply a single sales factor apportionment formula for most businesses starting in tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2011. </font><font style="display: inline;">For tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2013, California Proposition 39 changes the California default apportionment filing method to the single sales factor method. </font><font style="display: inline;">As a result, we revalued our California deferred tax assets expected to be realized.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">The a</font><font style="display: inline;">uthoritative guidance of income taxes provides guidance on the financial statement recognition and measurement of a tax position taken or expected to be taken in a tax return, and clarifies the accounting for uncertainty in income taxes recognized in the financial statements. This authoritative guidance also provides guidance on derecognition, classification, interest and penalties, accounting in interim periods, disclosures, and transition. This authoritative guidance requires significant judgment in determining what constitutes an individual tax position as well as assessing the outcome of each tax position. Changes in judgment as to recognition or measurement of tax positions can materially affect the estimate of the effective tax rate, and consequently affect our operating results. </font><font style="display: inline;">The reserve amount associated with this authoritative guidance was determined with considerable judgment and estimation, and is continuously monitored by management based on the best information available including changes in tax regulations, the outcome of relevant court cases, ongoing tax audits, and other information. During the </font><font style="display: inline;">fiscal </font><font style="display: inline;">year ended </font><font style="display: inline;">March 30, 2013</font><font style="display: inline;">, the liability for uncertain tax positions less accrued interest and penalties decreased </font><font style="display: inline;">from </font><font style="display: inline;">$3,661,000 to $3,</font><font style="display: inline;">160,000. Of the total $3,</font><font style="display: inline;">160,000 of uncertain tax benefits, $2,275,000 </font><font style="display: inline;">represents the amount that if recognized, would favorably affect the effective income tax rate in any future periods. We cannot conclude on the range of cash payments that will be made within the next twelve months associated with our uncertain tax positions.</font>
		</p>

		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;;font-size: 11pt"><font style="display: inline;">Our available-for-sale portfolio in fiscal 201</font><font style="display: inline;">3</font><font style="display: inline;"> includes </font><font style="display: inline;">municipal bonds, corporate bonds, ARS, </font><font style="display: inline;">government agency bonds, commercial papers</font><font style="display: inline;"> and certificates of deposits.&nbsp;&nbsp;These securities are reported at fair value. </font><font style="display: inline;">The ARS held by us are primarily backed by pools of student loans and</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">a significant portion of them are collateralized and</font><font style="display: inline;"> guaranteed</font><font style="display: inline;"> by the United States Department of Education. </font><font style="display: inline;">Until February 2012,</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">all of our </font><font style="display: inline;">ARS </font><font style="display: inline;">were</font><font style="display: inline;"> rated by the major independent rating agencies as</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">either AAA or Aaa</font><font style="display: inline;">.&nbsp; </font><font style="display: inline;">However, one of our ARS holdings was downgraded by Standard and Poor's (&#x201C;S&amp;P&#x201D;)</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">in February 2012 to AA+, then in June 2012 to A with a negative outlook and in May 2013 to A with a watch negative by Fitch. Also in May 2013, the other ARS was downgraded from AAA to AAA with a watch negative by Fitch. </font><font style="display: inline;">Due to the lack of availability of observable market quotes on our investment portfolio of ARS, the fair value was estimated based on a discounted cash flow model and included a discount factor for illiquidity of the ARS market. The assumptions used in the discounted cash flow model include estimates for interest rates, timing and amounts of cash flows, liquidity of the underlying security, expected holding periods and contractual terms of the security</font><font style="display: inline;">.&nbsp;&nbsp;We concluded that the fair value of our ARS was $13,800,000, or 91.7% of their par value of $15,050,000 as of March 30, 2013, and accordingly recorded a temporary impairment of $1,250,000. </font><font style="display: inline;">We review our securities for impairments in accordance with the authoritative guidance and other related guidance</font><font style="display: inline;"> issued by the</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">Financial Accounting Standard Board (&#x201C;</font><font style="display: inline;">FASB</font><font style="display: inline;">&#x201D;)</font><font style="display: inline;"> in order to determine the classification of the impairment as &#x201C;temporary&#x201D; or &#x201C;other-than-temporary.&#x201D; Declines in fair value that are considered other-than-temporary are charged to the Statement of Income and those that are considered temporary are reported as a component of accumulated other comprehensive income (loss) in shareholders&#x2019; equity.</font>

		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-weight:bold;">Recent Developments</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">We operate in the highly cyclical global semiconductor market, evidenced by fluctuating demand cycles for our products. During the post 2008 recession period, which for us began in the second half of fiscal 2010, our sales increased from $66.7 million in fiscal 2010 to $83.2 million in fiscal 2011, as end user demand increased for medical ultrasound products, telecom optical MEMS drivers and LED drivers for general lighting. Additionally, for many of our products sales increased to support replenishment of distributor and customer inventories. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">During fiscal 2012 and 2013 sales decreased to $65.5 million and $61.0 million, respectively. In fiscal 2012 our LCD TV LED backlighting customer began to supply its own needs in-house; we experienced softness in demand in our medical ultrasound products; there were down cycles in telecom optical MEMS drivers and other telecom products; and our customer&#x2019;s cell phone application using our EL inverters had declining sales. In fiscal 2013 we experienced softness in demand for a significant medical ultrasound custom product and several industrial products stemming from overall market softness and product transitions. Additionally, orders for a high volume military display IC were cut in the second quarter. Mitigating these sales reductions were increases in LED backlighting drivers and a resurgence in demand for telecom optical MEMS drivers.&nbsp;&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">During fiscal 2012 and 2013 we launche</font><font style="display: inline;">d &nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">almost 50</font><font style="display: inline;"> new pr</font><font style="display: inline;">oducts, several of which our customers have designed into Medical, LED and Printer applications that we expect will generate material sales. In part from these new products, we believe we will grow</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">sales in LED general and backlighting ICs, Printer drivers and Medical ultrasound products so that our quarterly sales will exceed $17.6 million in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2014, although no assurance can be given.&nbsp; </font>

					<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 0.05pt;text-align:right;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">

					<p style="margin:0pt 0.15pt 0.05pt 0pt;text-align:right;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">

		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">We have a broad base of customers, which in some cases manufacture end products spanning multiple markets.&nbsp;&nbsp;As such, the assignment of revenue to the aforementioned markets requires the use of estimates, judgment, and extrapolation.&nbsp;&nbsp;Actual results may differ from those reported.&nbsp; </font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Overall, our sales declined approximately $4.5 million, or 7% due to declines in sales to the medical electronics, printers/EL, and industrial/other markets which were partially offset by increases in sales to the LED lighting and telecom markets.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Our sales to the medical electronics market accounted for 39% of total sales in fiscal 2013 and decreased 10% compared to the prior fiscal year. This sales decrease was primarily due to reduced shipments of a custom product. This reduction was partially offset by increased custom processing services. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">In recent years, the overall ultrasound market has been shifting from big console systems to transportable and hand- held ultrasound imaging units, which has driven the ultrasound imaging market growth along with product upgrades for cart-based consoles and large stationary systems.&nbsp;&nbsp;Because of space and power constraints, there are more requirements for integration, and with our high voltage IC technology we have been among the most qualified to support these requirements. Geographically, the imaging equipment market is expanding very rapidly in China, India and many African countries.&nbsp;&nbsp;Traditionally, OEMs in the United States, Germany, and Japan have been the main developers and manufacturers of medical ultrasound imaging machines to whom we have sold our products successfully.&nbsp;&nbsp;Companies in those regions continue to grow and develop new machines although most of them have moved their operations to Asia to reduce cost. Today we see significant opportunities with Chinese and Korean medical ultrasound imaging machine companies. We are expanding our product development activities and product offerings to capitalize on these exciting market growth opportunities.&nbsp;&nbsp;Through the introduction of our new integrated solutions complemented by our discrete transistor and array building block product offerings, we believe we will continue to be a major player in this business.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">We have recently launched several analog switches that are designed into new medical ultrasound systems. We expect sales of these new products to begin in the second half of fiscal 2014.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">In fiscal 2013, sales to the printers/EL market,</font><font style="display: inline;"> which largely consist of EL inverter ICs, commercial printing ICs, display ICs and custom processing services,</font><font style="display: inline;"> decreased 14% compared to the prior year. This reduction is primarily </font>
		</p>
		<p><font size="1"> </font></p><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:0pt;text-align:center;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">

			<font style="display: inline;">24</font>

		</p>

			&nbsp;

		</p>

		<p style="margin:0pt;text-align:center;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">

			<font style="display: inline;font-weight:bold;font-size:10pt;"> &nbsp; &nbsp;</font>

		</p>

		<p style="margin:0pt;text-align:center;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">

			&nbsp;

		</p>

		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">

			<font style="text-indent:0pt;margin-left:0pt; width:193.5pt;"></font><font style="text-indent:0pt;margin-left:0pt; width:-1pt;text-align:left"><font style="display: inline;font-weight:bold;"></font><font style="display: inline;font-weight:bold;"></font></font>

		</p>

</div>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;;font-size: 11pt"><font style="display: inline;">attributable to lower sales of an IC for a military application which declined significantly after the first fiscal quarter of 2013 and due to a softening of demand for several display and EL drivers. Partially offsetting these declines was an increase in sales of drivers for a new printer application used </font><font style="display: inline;">to print on</font><font style="display: inline;"> ceramics and fabrics. These drivers can also be used in 3D printing applications. We expect growth in sales for fiscal 2014 from printer head drivers being designed into these and other new printing applications.&nbsp;&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">We began shipping printer head drivers into an OLED market manufacturing application in fiscal 2012 and continued supplying ICs for our customers&#x2019; prototype equipment in fiscal 2013. If our customers transition to volume production during fiscal 2014, we would have additional growth in sales compared to fiscal 2013.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Sales to the industrial/other market decreased 21% in fiscal 2013 compared to fiscal 2012 primarily due to reduced unit volumes of our ICs and DMOS transistors resulting mainly from competition and our transition from older to newer product versions.&nbsp;&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Sales to the LED lighting market increased 24% compared to the prior fiscal year.&nbsp; In December, 2012 we began shipping our high voltage LED driver IC for a series of LED TVs. Additionally, unit shipments of our ICs for a high-end monitor nearly doubled with a favorable mix of high end versus low end chips.&nbsp;&nbsp;We expect shipments of our LED backlighting and general lighting drivers to increase in fiscal 2014 compared to fiscal 2013, which will drive increases in our overall sales to the LED lighting market.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Sales to the telecom market in fiscal 2013 increased 30% compared to the prior fiscal year.&nbsp; This increase in sales was due to increased shipments of our </font><font style="display: inline;">high voltage driver ICs for optical MEMS applications.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Our current growth strategy relies on our ability to continuously and successfully introduce and market new innovative products that meet our customers&#x2019; requirements.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">

			<font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">R&amp;D expenses include payroll and benefits, processing costs, and depreciation. We also expense prototype </font><font style="display: inline;">experimental </font><font style="display: inline;">wafers and mask sets related to new products </font><font style="display: inline;">development </font><font style="display: inline;">as R&amp;D expenses.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">The year-over-year decrease of $423,000 in R&amp;D expense was primarily due to reduced expenses for experimental engineering runs of $322,000, and lower depreciation expense of $178,000, partially offset by an increase&nbsp;&nbsp;in the fair value of our</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">Non-Qualified Deferred Compensation Plan (&#x201C;NQDCP&#x201D;) assets. This increase corresponds to an increase in the NQDCP liability. To recognize an increase or decrease in the NQDCP plan assets, we record the difference in fair value to other income (expense) net. Correspondingly, to recognize an increase or decrease in the NQDCP liability, the Company records the difference to other benefits expense which impacts R&amp;D expense to the extent the investments are beneficially owned by R&amp;D employees.</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">The increase in percentage of net sales is primarily due to the decreased sales. R&amp;D expenses may fluctuate both in absolute dollars and as a percentage of sales; for example, R&amp;D expenses would increase if we have a large number of R&amp;D projects that are in the protot</font><font style="display: inline;">ype wafer stage and/or if profit-sharing accruals increase. We expect R&amp;D spending in fiscal year 2014 to increase and be between 18% and 22% of net sales.</font><font style="display: inline;"> &nbsp; &nbsp;</font>
		</p>

		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">SG&amp;A expenses consist primarily of employee related expenses, commissions to sales representatives, occupancy expenses including expenses associated with our regional sales offices, cost of advertising and publications, and outside services such as legal, auditing, tax and compliance services related to Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">The increase of $297,000 in SG&amp;A expenses resulted primarily from increased expense related to our NQDCP as the plan assets increased in fair value by $427,000 compared to $177,000 during fiscal 2012. This&nbsp;&nbsp;increase&nbsp;&nbsp;corresponds to an increase in the NQDCP liability. To recognize the increase or decrease in the NQDCP plan assets, we record the difference in fair value to other income (expense) net. Correspondingly, to recognize the increase or decrease in the NQDCP liability, we record the difference to other benefits expense which impacts SG&amp;A expense to the extent the investments are beneficially owned by SG&amp;A employees.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">SG&amp;A expenses may fluctuate both in absolute dollars and as a percentage of sales; for example, SG&amp;A expenses would increase if commissionable sales increase and/or if profit-sharing accruals increase.</font>

		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">We have a broad base of customers, which in some cases manufacture end products spanning multiple markets.&nbsp;&nbsp;As such, the assignment of revenue to the aforementioned markets requires the use of estimates, judgment, and extrapolation.&nbsp;&nbsp;Actual results may differ from those reported.&nbsp; </font><font style="display: inline;">During the first fiscal quarter of 2012 we reviewed our assignment of products to markets and made minor adjustments to the market assignment for certain DMOS products for both fiscal 2011 and 2012. Additionally, we renamed the &#x201C;imaging&#x201D; market &#x201C;EL/printers&#x201D; to avoid confusion with the medical imaging market.</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">The 21% decrease in net sales compared to the prior fiscal year was </font><font style="display: inline;">primarily due to </font><font style="display: inline;">decreases in sales of our LED driver ICs for backlighting LCD TVs</font><font style="display: inline;"> as our major customer began insourcing these drivers in the third fiscal quarter of 2011 which continued in fiscal 2012; reduced end user demand for and price erosion of medical ultrasound products; a slowdown in demand for optical MEMS drivers; </font><font style="display: inline;">declining sales of our customer&#x2019;s cell phone application using our EL inverters;</font><font style="display: inline;"> and reduced sales of our custom processing services.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Our sales to the medical electronics market accounted for 40% of total sales in fiscal 2012 and decreased 13% compared to the prior fiscal year. This sales decrease was due to lower shipments of our analog switches and high voltage pulser ICs and chipsets resulting primarily from reduced end demand and from price erosion due to increased competition. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Due to the global economic improvement following the 2008 recession, the demand for medical ultrasound imaging machines picked up starting in our fourth quarter of fiscal 2010 and continued through the second quarter of fiscal 2011. However, in addition to our normal seasonal decline in the third and fourth quarters, we experienced declines resulting from the impact of increased competition. In the first half of fiscal 2012, sales improved modestly and then declined in the third fiscal quarter following a normal seasonal pattern. Medical ultrasound sales then surged higher in our fourth fiscal quarter. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">In fiscal 2012, sales to the printers/EL market,</font><font style="display: inline;"> which largely consist of EL inverter ICs, commercial printing ICs, display ICs and custom processing services,</font><font style="display: inline;"> increased 1% compared to the prior year. </font><font style="display: inline;">We began shipping into an OLED market manufacturing application in fiscal 2012 and sales of our display and commercial printing ICs increased resulting from the improved economy.&nbsp;&nbsp;Additionally, we had higher sales of a product used in a military application. Nearly offsetting these increases was a reduction in sales of EL driver ICs for backlighting cell phone keypads, as our customer&#x2019;s shipments of its cellphones using these keypads declined. We are one of the key providers of EL driver ICs for backlighting cell phones, hand-held instruments and watches, and the leading supplier in the high-end industrial printer market with both standard and custom products. </font>
		</p>

		</p>

</div>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;;font-size: 11pt"><font style="display: inline;">Sales to the industrial/other market decreased 19% in fiscal 2012 compared to fiscal 2011 primarily due to reduced sales of our custom processing services and to a lesser extent due to reduced sales of our ICs and DMOS transistors resulting from a softening of the overall economy. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Sales to the LED lighting market decreased 50% compared to the prior fiscal year.&nbsp; This decrease resulted from a reduction in shipments of our high voltage LED driver ICs for LED TVs as our major LCD TV customer began supplying a substantial portion of its requirements of LED drivers internally starting in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2011 which continued throughout fiscal 2012 and from the global slowdown of TV sales. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Sales to the telecom market in fiscal 2012 decreased 51% compared to the prior fiscal year.&nbsp; This decrease in sales was primarily due to reduced shipments of our </font><font style="display: inline;">high voltage driver ICs for optical MEMS applications.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Our principal geographic markets are in Asia, the U.S., and Europe. Sales by geographic regions as well as year-over-year percentage changes were as follows. The sales amounts are based on where we ship our products to, rather than where the customers&#x2019; headquarters are located. </font>

			<font style="display: inline;font-size:10pt;"></font><font style="display: inline;">Net sales to international customers in fiscal 2012 were </font><font style="display: inline;">$42,593,000, or 65% </font><font style="display: inline;">of our net sales as compared to </font><font style="display: inline;">$58,868,000 or 71% </font><font style="display: inline;">of net sales for the prior fiscal year</font><font style="display: inline;">.&nbsp;This decrease in international net sales resulted from</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">our major LCD TV customer supplying a substantial portion of its requirements of LED drivers for LED backlighting internally starting in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2011 which continued throughout fiscal 2012 and from the global slowdown of TV sales</font><font style="display: inline;">; reduced end user demand and price erosion in medical ultrasound products; and declining sales by our customer for a cell phone application using our EL inverters. </font>

		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;">Cost of Sales and Gross Profit</font><font style="display: inline;"> &nbsp; &nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Gross profit represents net sales less cost of sales.&nbsp;&nbsp;Cost of sales includes the cost of purchasing raw silicon wafers; costs associated with assembly, packaging, test, quality assurance and product yields; the cost of personnel, facilities, and equipment associated with manufacturing support; and net charges for excess or obsolete inventory.&nbsp; </font>

		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">R&amp;D expenses include payroll and benefits, processing costs, and depreciation. We also expense prototype experimental wafers and mask sets related to new products development as R&amp;D expenses.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">The year-over-year decrease of $452,000 in R&amp;D expense was primarily due to reduced expense of $173,000 related to our Non-Qualified Deferred Compensation Plan (&#x201C;NQDCP&#x201D;) as the Plan assets increased in fair value by $43,000 compared to $216,000 during fiscal 2011, lower employee stock compensation expense of $123,000, reduced engineering supplies, masks and workplates expenses of $97,000, and lower depreciation of $88,000. An increase or decrease in the fair value of our NQDCP assets corresponds to an increase or decrease in the NQDCP liability. To recognize the increase or decrease in the NQDCP plan assets, we record the difference in fair value to other income (expense) net. Correspondingly, to recognize the increase or decrease in the NQDCP liability, the Company records the difference to other benefits expense which impacts R&amp;D expense to the extent the investments are beneficially owned by R&amp;D employees.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">The increase in percentage of net sales is primarily due to the decreased sales. R&amp;D expenses may fluctuate both in absolute dollars and as a percentage of sales; for example, R&amp;D expenses would increase if we have a large number of R&amp;D projects that are in the prototype wafer stage and/or if profit-sharing accruals increase. </font>
		</p>

			<font style="display: inline;">SG&amp;A expenses consist primarily of employee related expenses, commissions to sales representatives, occupancy expenses including expenses associated with our regional sales offices, cost of advertising and publications, and outside services such as legal, auditing, tax and compliance services related to Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002. </font>
