		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">The decrease of $1,354,000 in SG&amp;A expenses resulted primarily from lower professional services costs for audit, legal and consulting services of $898,000, reduced sales incentives expense of $371,000, and reduced expense of $205,000 related to our Non-Qualified Deferred Compensation Plan (&#x201C;NQDCP&#x201D;) as the Plan assets increased in fair value by $177,000 compared to $382,000 during fiscal 2011. An increase or decrease in the fair value of our NQDCP assets corresponds to an increase or decrease in the NQDCP liability. To recognize the increase or decrease in the NQDCP plan assets, we record the difference in fair value to other income (expense) net. Correspondingly, to recognize the increase or decrease in the NQDCP liability, we record the difference to other benefits expense which impacts SG&amp;A expense to the extent the investments are beneficially owned by SG&amp;A employees. </font>

			<font style="display: inline;">Operating Activities</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Net cash provided by operating activities is net income adjusted for certain non-cash items and changes in assets and liabilities. The increase of $6,454,000 compared to the prior year resulted from an increase of changes in assets and liabilities totaling $11,073,000, partially offset by lesser net income after non cash adjustments of $4,619,000. Net income was lower than the prior year by $502,000, while non-cash adjustments to net income were lower by $4,117,000. The decreased non-cash adjustments to net income resulted primarily from a decrease in provision for excess and obsolete inventories driven by an increase in demand by our customers in the first half of fiscal 2013 compared to the second half of fiscal 2012, lesser depreciation expense compared to last year, a higher gain from trading investments, less amortization </font><font style="display: inline;">of premium on short-term investments</font><font style="display: inline;"> and a lesser stock based compensation expense.</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">Changes in operating assets and liabilities increased cash provided by operating activities due to a substantial reduction in prepaid expenses and other assets compared to an increase in the prior year due to prepaid taxes in the prior year versus large tax refund in the current year; a reduction in income taxes payable, a decrease in trade accounts payable and accrued liabilities; and an increase in deferred revenue as our distributor channel inventory increased. We received tax refunds of $4,284,000 during this fiscal year. These increases to cash were partially offset by a reduction in prepaid income taxes.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-weight:bold;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Investing Activities</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Investing cash flows consist primarily of capital expenditures and purchases of short-term investments, partially offset by sales of short-term investments and redemptions of long-term investments. Cash used in investing activities was $</font><font style="display: inline;">2</font><font style="display: inline;">,</font><font style="display: inline;">0</font><font style="display: inline;">90,000 in fiscal year 2013 compared to $232,000 in fiscal year 2012.&nbsp;&nbsp;Our purchases of investments were $1,</font><font style="display: inline;">4</font><font style="display: inline;">42,000 greater than disposals of investments, and our investment in capital expenditure was $655,000. Largely offsetting this were ARS redemptions at par totaling $13,000,000, which were the source of funds for our short-term investment purchases. Our capital expenditures in fiscal 2013 were devoted primarily to upgrade our test capacity and IT related equipment.&nbsp;&nbsp; </font>
		</p>

			<font style="display: inline;">As further described in Note 3, auction failures have limited and we expect will continue to limit our ability to </font><font style="display: inline;">fully </font><font style="display: inline;">liquidate our ARS for some period of time. However, we do not believe the auction failures will materially impact our ability to fund our working capital needs, capital expenditures, or other business requirements. As of March 30, 2013, our ARS investments had declined to a par value of $15,050,000 and we had approximately $152,998,000 of working capital, including approximately $140,261,000 of cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments, and we have generated cash from our operations for the past several years.</font><font style="display: inline;"> Subsequent to March 30, 2013, we received two ARS redemptions at par value totaling $12,950,000.</font>

Net cash used by financing activities in fiscal 2013 was $19,602,000 due to repurchases of our shares from the open market totaling $8,673,000 and payment of a special dividend of $11,523,000, offset in small part by $594,000 of proceeds associated with the exercise of stock options and employee purchases through the employee stock purchase plan. The decrease of $4,963,000 compared to the prior year resulted from lesser net income after non-cash adjustments of $6,987,000, partially offset by an increase from changes in assets and liabilities totaling $2,024,000. Net income was lower than the prior year by $7,533,000, while non-cash adjustments to net income were higher by $546,000. The increased non-cash adjustments to net income resulted primarily from an increase in provision for excess and obsolete inventories due to a reduction in demand for the Company&#x2019;s products compared to </font><font style="display: inline;">the prior </font><font style="display: inline;">year, partially offset by a greater decrease in deferred income taxes. Changes in operating assets and liabilities increased cash provided by operating activities due to a reduction in inventories compared to a large increase in the prior year as we reduced capacity utilization of our wafer fab more than our sales declined; a decrease in prepaid taxes compared to an increase last year as our tax liability was reduced; a lesser increase in trade accounts payable and accrued liabilities; and a decrease in deferred revenue. These increases to cash were partially offset by a reduction in income taxes payable compared to an increase </font><font style="display: inline;">in the prior </font><font style="display: inline;">year, an increase in prepaid expenses and other assets compared to a decrease </font><font style="display: inline;">in fiscal 2011</font><font style="display: inline;">; trade accounts receivable being flat compared to a large decrease at the end of last year as sales declined; a decrease in trade accounts payable and accrued expenses compared to an increase </font><font style="display: inline;">in fiscal 2011</font><font style="display: inline;">; and a decrease in deferred revenue compared to an increase </font><font style="display: inline;">in the prior </font><font style="display: inline;">year as our distributor channel reduced inventory </font><font style="display: inline;">in fiscal 2012</font><font style="display: inline;">.</font>

		<p style="margin:0pt;font-weight:bold;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Recent Accounting Pronouncements</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">In February 2013, Financial Accounting Standard Board (&#x201C;FASB&#x201D;) issued an amendment regarding net income or other comprehensive income in financial statements.&nbsp;&nbsp;This amendment does not change the current requirements for reporting net income or other comprehensive income in financial statements.&nbsp;&nbsp;However, it requires an entity to provide information about the amounts reclassified out of accumulated other comprehensive income by component. In addition, an entity is required to present, either on the face of the statement where net income is presented or in the notes, significant amounts reclassified out of accumulated other comprehensive income by the respective line items of net income but only if the amount reclassified is required under U.S. GAAP to be reclassified to net income in its entirety in the same reporting period. For other amounts that are not required under U.S. GAAP to be reclassified in their entirety to net income, an entity is required to cross-reference to other disclosures required under U.S. GAAP that provide additional detail about those amounts.&nbsp;&nbsp;This amendment is effective prospectively for reporting periods beginning after December 15, 2012 (the fiscal quarter ending June 29, 2013 for us).&nbsp;&nbsp;We are currently assessing the potential effect to our consolidated financial statements in applying this guidance.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;line-height:12pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 12pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">In June 2011, Financial Accounting Standard Board (&#x201C;FASB&#x201D;) issued new authoritative guidance regarding Presentation of Comprehensive Income.&nbsp;&nbsp;This amendment attempts to improve comparability, consistency, and transparency of financial reporting and to increase the prominence of items reported in other comprehensive income.&nbsp;&nbsp;In order to facilitate convergence with International Financial Reporting Standards (&#x201C;IFRS&#x201D;), FASB has decided to eliminate the option to present components of other comprehensive income as part of the statement of changes in shareholders&#x2019; equity.&nbsp;&nbsp;Also, this amendment requires that all non-owner changes in shareholders&#x2019; equity be presented in a single continuous statement of comprehensive income or in two separate but consecutive statements.&nbsp;&nbsp;This amendment is effective for annual periods beginning after December&nbsp;15, 2011 and interim periods within these fiscal years (the fiscal quarter ended June 30, 2012 for us) and is applied retrospectively.&nbsp;&nbsp;On October 21, 2011, the FASB proposed a deferral of the requirement to present reclassifications of other comprehensive income on the face of the income statement. Companies would still be required to adopt all other requirements contained in the guidance</font><font style="display: inline;font-size:12pt;">.</font><font style="display: inline;font-weight:bold;font-size:12pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">The adoption of these amended standards affected the presentation of other comprehensive income, as we have elected to present two separate but consecutive statements, but did not have an effect on our financial position or results of operations.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-weight:bold;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Item 7A.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures about Market Risk</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-weight:bold;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Interest Rate Risk</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt 0.7pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">We are exposed to financial market risks primarily due to changes in interest rates.&nbsp;&nbsp;We do not use derivatives to alter the interest characteristics of our investment securities.&nbsp;&nbsp;We have no holdings of derivative or commodity instruments, and our holdings are for purposes other than trading.&nbsp;&nbsp;Our investment portfolio is primarily comprised of </font><font style="display: inline;">municipal bonds, corporate bonds, ARS, </font><font style="display: inline;">government agency bonds, commercial papers</font><font style="display: inline;"> and certificates of deposits</font><font style="display: inline;">.&nbsp;&nbsp;Investments and cash and cash equivalents generated interest income </font><font style="display: inline;">of $</font><font style="display: inline;">1,250</font><font style="display: inline;">,000 and $</font><font style="display: inline;">999</font><font style="display: inline;">,000 </font><font style="display: inline;">in fiscal year</font><font style="display: inline;">s</font><font style="display: inline;"> 201</font><font style="display: inline;">3</font><font style="display: inline;"> and 20</font><font style="display: inline;">12</font><font style="display: inline;">, respectively.&nbsp;&nbsp;Based on our investments and cash and cash equivalent balance as of </font><font style="display: inline;">March 30, 2013</font><font style="display: inline;">, one percentage point change in interest rates would cause change in our annual interest income </font><font style="display: inline;">by</font><font style="display: inline;"> an amount of approximately </font><font style="display: inline;">$1,</font><font style="display: inline;">453</font><font style="display: inline;">,000.</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">ARS are subject to the risk that the secondary market might fail to provide the liquidity opportunity at the rate reset points. This risk, which we have encountered with regard to our ARS, manifests itself in sponsoring broker-dealers withdrawing from the auction process that provides the rate reset and liquidity. We recorded </font><font style="display: inline;">a $</font><font style="display: inline;">1</font><font style="display: inline;">,</font><font style="display: inline;">2</font><font style="display: inline;">50,000</font><font style="display: inline;"> temporary impairment in value as of </font><font style="display: inline;">March 30, 2013</font><font style="display: inline;">, &nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">which </font><font style="display: inline;">decreased from </font><font style="display: inline;">$</font><font style="display: inline;">2,150</font><font style="display: inline;">,000</font><font style="display: inline;"> as of </font><font style="display: inline;">March 31, 2012, due to our reduced ARS holdings resulting from several ARS redemptions</font><font style="display: inline;">. In the event we need to access the funds associated with failed auctions, they are not expected to be accessible until one of the following occurs: a successful auction occurs, the issuer redeems the issue, a buyer is found outside of the auction process or the underlying securities have matured.</font>
		</p>

		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;;font-size: 11pt"><font style="display: inline;">The ARS we h</font><font style="display: inline;">o</font><font style="display: inline;">ld ha</font><font style="display: inline;">d</font><font style="display: inline;"> contractual maturities generally </font><font style="display: inline;">between </font><font style="display: inline;">2</font><font style="display: inline;">4</font><font style="display: inline;"> to </font><font style="display: inline;">28</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;years</font><font style="display: inline;"> and had a total par value of </font><font style="display: inline;">$</font><font style="display: inline;">15,050</font><font style="display: inline;">,000 as of </font><font style="display: inline;">March 30, 2013</font><font style="display: inline;">, compared to $</font><font style="display: inline;">28,050</font><font style="display: inline;">,000 as of </font><font style="display: inline;">March 31, 2012</font><font style="display: inline;">. They </font><font style="display: inline;">are</font><font style="display: inline;"> in the form of auction rate bonds backed by a pool of student loans, whose interest rates were reset every seven to thirty-five days through an auction process prior to the fourth quarter of fiscal 2008. At the end of each reset period, investors can sell or continue to hold the securities at par. The ARS held by us are backed by student loans and </font><font style="display: inline;">of high credit quality and a significant portion of them are collater</font><font style="display: inline;">al</font><font style="display: inline;">ized and </font><font style="display: inline;">are guaranteed by the United States Department of Education. </font><font style="display: inline;">Until February 2012</font><font style="display: inline;">, all </font><font style="display: inline;">of our </font><font style="display: inline;">ARS </font><font style="display: inline;">were</font><font style="display: inline;"> rated by the major independent rating agencies as either AAA or Aaa. </font><font style="display: inline;">However, one of our ARS holdings was downgraded by S&amp;P in February 2012 to AA+, then in June 2012 to A with a negative outlook </font><font style="display: inline;">and was downgraded by Fitch in May 2013 to A with a watch negative. </font><font style="display: inline;">Also in May 2013, the other ARS was downgraded from AAA to AAA with a watch negative</font><font style="display: inline;"> by Fitch.</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">We belie</font><font style="display: inline;">ve these downgrades had no impact on the fair value</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">of this ARS as of March 30, 2013. </font><font style="display: inline;">As </font><font style="display: inline;">all of </font><font style="display: inline;">our ARS are of high credit rating, we believe the credit risk is very low.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;line-height:12pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Subsequent to March 30, 2013, one of our ARS </font><font style="display: inline;">was fully redeemed at par value of $12,800,000 and our other ARS wa</font><font style="display: inline;">s partially redeemed at par valu</font><font style="display: inline;">e of $150,000. The combined redemptions </font><font style="display: inline;">reduc</font><font style="display: inline;">ed</font><font style="display: inline;"> our ARS holdings </font><font style="display: inline;">from a par value of $15,050,000 </font><font style="display: inline;">to $2,100,000.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">If the issuer of the ARS is unable to successfully close future auctions or does not redeem the ARS, or the United States government fails to support its guaranty of the obligations, we may be required to adjust the carrying value of the ARS and record other-than-temporary impairment charges in future periods, which could materially affect our results of operations and financial condition. </font><font style="display: inline;">However, w</font><font style="display: inline;">e expect that we will receive the principal associated with these </font><font style="display: inline;">ARS</font><font style="display: inline;"> through one of the means described above.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-weight:bold;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Foreign Currency Exchange Risks</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">We do not hedge any potential risk from foreign currency exposure. </font><font style="display: inline;">With our operations in Hong Kong, we face exposure to an adverse change in the exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar.&nbsp;&nbsp;We believe that our exposure is relatively small, thus we do not employ hedging techniques designed to mitigate this foreign currency exposure.&nbsp;&nbsp;Likewise, we could experience unanticipated currency gains or losses.&nbsp;&nbsp;As the level of activity at this operation changes over time, actual currency gains or losses could have an adverse impact to the Consolidated Financial Statements.</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">Our</font><font style="display: inline;"> foreign sales are denominated in United States dollars.&nbsp;&nbsp;Currency exchange fluctuations in countries where </font><font style="display: inline;">we do</font><font style="display: inline;"> business could harm the business by resulting in pricing that is not competitive with prices denominated in local currencies.</font>
		</p>

		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-weight:bold;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Item </font><font style="display: inline;">9A</font><font style="display: inline;">.&nbsp;&nbsp;Controls and Procedures</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">(a)</font><font style="display: inline;;font-size:12pt;font-family:Times New Roman;text-indent:0pt;margin-left:0pt;width:36pt">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;"></font><font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;">Evaluation of Disclosure Controls and Procedures</font><font style="display: inline;">.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;text-decoration:underline;">(i) Disclosure Controls and Procedures</font><font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;">. &nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">We maintain disclosure controls and procedures (as defined in Exchange Act Rules 13a-15(e) and 15d-15(e)) that are designed to ensure that information required to be disclosed by us in reports that we file or submit under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 is recorded, processed, summarized, and reported within the time periods specified in the SEC's rules and forms, and that such information is accumulated and communicated to our management, including our chief executive officer and chief financial officer, as appropriate to allow timely decisions regarding required disclosures. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;text-decoration:underline;">(ii) Limitations on the Effectiveness of Disclosure Controls</font><font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;">.&nbsp; </font><font style="display: inline;">In designing and evaluating our disclosure controls and procedures, management recognized that disclosure controls and procedures, no matter how well conceived and operated, can provide only reasonable, not absolute, assurance that the objectives of the disclosure controls and procedures are met taking into account the totality of the circumstances. Additionally, in designing disclosure </font>
		</p>
		<p><font size="1"> </font></p><div style="width:100%">

		</p>

</div>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;;font-size: 11pt"><font style="display: inline;">controls and procedures, our management necessarily was required to apply its judgment in evaluating the cost-benefit relationship of possible disclosure controls and procedures.&nbsp;&nbsp;The design of any disclosure controls and procedures is also based in part upon certain assumptions about the likelihood of future events, and there can be no assurance that any design will succeed in achieving its stated goals under all potential future conditions. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;text-decoration:underline;">(iii) Evaluation of Disclosure Controls and Procedures. </font><font style="display: inline;">Our chief executive officer and chief financial officer have evaluated our disclosure controls and procedures as of </font><font style="display: inline;">March 30, 2013</font><font style="display: inline;">, and have determined that they are effective at the reasonable assurance level. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">(b)</font><font style="display: inline;;font-size:12pt;font-family:Times New Roman;text-indent:0pt;margin-left:0pt;width:36pt">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;"></font><font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;">Management&#x2019;s Annual Report on Internal Control over Financial Reporting:&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Our management is responsible for establishing and maintaining adequate internal control over our financial reporting which is designed to provide reasonable assurance regarding the reliability of our financial reporting and the preparation of financial statements for external purposes in accordance with U.S. generally accepted accounting principles. Internal control over financial reporting includes those policies and procedures that: (i) pertain to the maintenance of records that, in reasonable detail, accurately and fairly reflect the transactions and dispositions of our assets; (ii) provide reasonable assurance that transactions are recorded as necessary to permit preparation of financial statements in accordance with U.S. generally accepted accounting principles, and that receipts and expenditures of the Company are being made only in accordance with authorizations of our management and directors; and (iii) provide reasonable assurance regarding prevention or timely detection of unauthorized acquisition, use or disposition of our assets that could have a material effect on the financial statements.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Our management with participation of our </font><font style="display: inline;">c</font><font style="display: inline;">hief </font><font style="display: inline;">e</font><font style="display: inline;">xecutive </font><font style="display: inline;">o</font><font style="display: inline;">fficer and our </font><font style="display: inline;">c</font><font style="display: inline;">hief </font><font style="display: inline;">f</font><font style="display: inline;">inancial </font><font style="display: inline;">o</font><font style="display: inline;">fficer, assessed the effectiveness of our internal control over financial reporting as of </font><font style="display: inline;">March 30, 2013</font><font style="display: inline;">.&nbsp;&nbsp;In making this assessment, our management used the criteria set forth by the Committee of Sponsoring Organizations of the Treadway Commission (&#x201C;COSO&#x201D;) in </font><font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;">Internal Control-Integrated Framework.&nbsp; </font><font style="display: inline;">Based on the assessment using those criteria, management concluded that, as of </font><font style="display: inline;">March 30, 2013</font><font style="display: inline;">, our internal control over financial reporting is effective.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">BDO USA, LLP</font><font style="display: inline;">, the independent registered public accounting firm that audited the consolidated financial statements </font><font style="display: inline;">as of and for the fiscal year ended March 30, 2013, </font><font style="display: inline;">included in this Annual Report on Form&nbsp;10-K, also audited and expressed an unqualified opinion on the effectiveness of our internal control over financial reporting as of </font><font style="display: inline;">March 30, 2013</font><font style="display: inline;">. &nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">T</font><font style="display: inline;">he report</font><font style="display: inline;">s</font><font style="display: inline;"> on the audit of internal control over financial reporting and the audit of the financial statements appear under item 15(a)(1) in this Annual Report on Form 10-K.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;text-align:justify;text-justify:inter-ideograph;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">(c)</font><font style="display: inline;;font-size:12pt;font-family:Times New Roman;text-indent:0pt;margin-left:0pt;width:36pt">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;"></font><font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;">Changes in Internal Control over Financial Reporting.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Our internal control over financial reporting (as defined in Exchange Act Rules 13a-15(f) and 15d-15(f)) is designed to provide reasonable assurance regarding the reliability of our financial reporting and preparation of financial statements for external purposes in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles. There were no changes in our internal control over financial reporting identified in connection with management&#x2019;s evaluation during the fourth quarter of fiscal 201</font><font style="display: inline;">3</font><font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">that have materially affected, or are reasonably likely to materially affect, our internal control over financial reporting.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;background-color: #FFFFFF;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">(d)</font><font style="display: inline;;font-size:12pt;font-family:Times New Roman;text-indent:0pt;margin-left:0pt;width:36pt">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;"></font><font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;">Inherent Limitations on Effectiveness of Controls</font><font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;">.</font><font style="display: inline;font-weight:bold;"> &nbsp; &nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;background-color: #FFFFFF;line-height:normal;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 10.1pt 5pt 0pt;background-color: #FFFFFF;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Our management, including our </font><font style="display: inline;">c</font><font style="display: inline;">hief </font><font style="display: inline;">e</font><font style="display: inline;">xecutive </font><font style="display: inline;">o</font><font style="display: inline;">fficer and our </font><font style="display: inline;">c</font><font style="display: inline;">hief </font><font style="display: inline;">f</font><font style="display: inline;">inancial </font><font style="display: inline;">o</font><font style="display: inline;">fficer, does not expect that our disclosure controls and procedures or our internal control over financial reporting will prevent or detect all errors and all fraud. Any control system, no matter how well designed and operated, can provide only reasonable, not absolute, assurance that the control system&#x2019;s objectives will be met. The design of a control system must reflect the fact that there are resource constraints and competing use of resources, and the benefits of controls must be considered relative to their costs in light of competing demands on limited resources.&nbsp;&nbsp;Further, because of the </font>
		</p>

		</p>

			&nbsp;

		</p>

			<font style="text-indent:0pt;margin-left:0pt; width:193.5pt;"></font><font style="text-indent:0pt;margin-left:0pt; width:-1pt;text-align:left"><font style="display: inline;font-weight:bold;"></font><font style="display: inline;font-weight:bold;"></font></font>

		</p>

</div>
		<p style="margin:0pt 10.1pt 5pt 0pt;background-color: #FFFFFF;font-family:Times New Roman;;font-size: 11pt"><font style="display: inline;">inherent limitations in all control systems, no evaluation of controls can provide absolute assurance that misstatements due to errors or frauds will not occur or that all control issues and instances of fraud, if any, within the company have been detected. These inherent limitations include the realities that judgments in decision-making can be faulty and that breakdowns can occur because of a simple error or mistake. Controls can also be circumvented by the individual acts or omissions of some persons, by collusion of two or more people, or by management override of the controls. The design of any system of controls is based in part on certain assumptions about the likelihood of future events, and there can be no assurance that any design will succeed in achieving its stated goals under all potential future conditions. Over time, controls may become inadequate because of changes in conditions or deterioration in the degree of compliance with policies or procedures. </font>

Under the 2009 Plan, the total number of shares of our common stock reserved for issuance consists of 1,000,000 shares plus (1) the 159,509 shares which remain authorized for issuance under the 2001 Plan but which were not subject to outstanding stock awards as of August 14, 2009, and (2) those of the 1,440,400 shares subject to stock awards outstanding under the 2001 Plan as of August 14, 2009, that terminate prior to exercise and would otherwise be returned to the share reserves under the 2001 Plan, with the total shares in addition to the 1,000,000 shares thus being up to a maximum of 1,599,909 shares. The 2009 Plan allows us to continue our prior option practices under the 2001 Plan to grant non-statutory options to key employees with an exercise price equal to the fair market value of our stock on the date of grant. Our options typically have a term of ten years and vest over five years, 20% on the first anniversary of the grant date and 20% at the end of each of the following four years. The 2009 Plan also provides us with the flexibility in designing equity incentives, including restricted stock awards, stock appreciation rights, restricted stock unit awards, performance stock awards, and performance cash awards. As of March 30, 2013, there were 797,151 shares remaining available for grant under the 2009 Plan.</font>

		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 12pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-size:12pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-size:10pt;">Board of Directors and Shareholders of</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-size:10pt;">Supertex, Inc.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-size:10pt;">Sunnyvale, California</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 12pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-size:12pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 12pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-size:12pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:18pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-size:10pt;">We have audited Supertex, Inc.&#x2019;s internal control over financial reporting as of </font><font style="display: inline;font-size:10pt;">March 30, 2013</font><font style="display: inline;font-size:10pt;">, based on criteria established in </font><font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;">Internal Control&nbsp;&#x2014;</font><font style="display: inline;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;font-size:10pt;">Integrated Framework</font><font style="display: inline;font-size:10pt;"> issued by the Committee of Sponsoring Organizations of the Treadway Commission (the COSO criteria). Supertex, Inc.&#x2019;s management is responsible for maintaining effective internal control over financial reporting and for its assessment of the effectiveness of internal control over financial reporting, included in the accompanying, &#x201C;Item&nbsp;9A, Management&#x2019;s Annual Report on Internal Control Over Financial Reporting and Attestation Report of the Registered Public Accounting Firm&#x201D;. Our responsibility is to express an opinion on the company&#x2019;s internal control over financial reporting based on our audit.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 12pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-size:12pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:18pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-size:10pt;">We conducted our audit in accordance with the standards of the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (United States). Those standards require that we plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance about whether effective internal control over financial reporting was maintained in all material respects. Our audit included obtaining an understanding of internal control over financial reporting, assessing the risk that a material weakness exists, and testing and evaluating the design and operating effectiveness of internal control based on the assessed risk. Our audit also included performing such other procedures as we considered necessary in the circumstances. We believe that our audit provides a reasonable basis for our opinion.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 12pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-size:12pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:18pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-size:10pt;">A company&#x2019;s internal control over financial reporting is a process designed to provide reasonable assurance regarding the reliability of financial reporting and the preparation of financial statements for external purposes in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles. A company&#x2019;s internal control over financial reporting includes those policies and procedures that (1)&nbsp;pertain to the maintenance of records that, in reasonable detail, accurately and fairly reflect the transactions and dispositions of the assets of the company; (2)&nbsp;provide reasonable assurance that transactions are recorded as necessary to permit preparation of financial statements in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles, and that receipts and expenditures of the company are being made only in accordance with authorizations of management and directors of the company; and (3)&nbsp;provide reasonable assurance regarding prevention or timely detection of unauthorized acquisition, use, or disposition of the company&#x2019;s assets that could have a material effect on the financial statements.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 12pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-size:12pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:18pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-size:10pt;">Because of its inherent limitations, internal control over financial reporting may not prevent or detect misstatements. Also, projections of any evaluation of effectiveness to future periods are subject to the risk that controls may become inadequate because of changes in conditions, or that the degree of compliance with the policies or procedures may deteriorate.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 12pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-size:12pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:18pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-size:10pt;">In our opinion, Supertex, Inc. maintained, in all material respects, effective internal control over financial reporting as of </font><font style="display: inline;font-size:10pt;">March 30, 2013</font><font style="display: inline;font-size:10pt;">, based on the COSO criteria.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 12pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-size:12pt;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;text-indent:18pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 10pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-size:10pt;">We also have audited, in accordance with the standards of the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (United States), the consolidated balance sheet</font><font style="display: inline;font-size:10pt;">s</font><font style="display: inline;font-size:10pt;"> of Supertex, Inc. as of </font><font style="display: inline;font-size:10pt;">March 30, 2013</font><font style="display: inline;font-size:10pt;"> and March 31, 2012</font><font style="display: inline;font-size:10pt;">, and the related consolidated statements of income, </font><font style="display: inline;font-size:10pt;">comprehensive income,</font><font style="display: inline;font-size:10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;font-size:10pt;">shareholders&#x2019;</font><font style="display: inline;font-size:10pt;"> equity and cash flows for the year</font><font style="display: inline;font-size:10pt;">s</font><font style="display: inline;font-size:10pt;"> then ended and our report dated </font><font style="display: inline;font-size:10pt;">June 12, 2013</font><font style="display: inline;font-size:10pt;"> expressed an unqualified opinion thereon.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;line-height:normal;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 12pt">

		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="text-indent:0pt;margin-left:0pt; width:225pt;"><font style="display: inline;">1.</font><a name="Financial_Footnotes"></a></font><font style="text-indent:0pt;margin-left:0pt; width:-1pt;text-align:left"><font style="display: inline;">NATURE OF BUSINESS AND SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES</font></font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;">Nature of Business</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Supertex, Inc. (together with its wholly-owned subsidiary, Supertex Limited, herein referred to as &#x201C;Supertex&#x201D; or the &#x201C;Company&#x201D;) designs, develops, manufactures, and markets high voltage analog and mixed signal integrated circuits utilizing high voltage DMOS, HVCMOS and HVBiCMOS analog and mixed signal technologies.&nbsp;&nbsp;The Company supplies standard and custom interface products primarily for use in the medical electronics</font><font style="display: inline;">,</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">LED lighting</font><font style="display: inline;">,</font><font style="display: inline;"> printers, devices using EL lamps</font><font style="display: inline;">, telecommunications</font><font style="display: inline;">, and industrial/other</font><font style="display: inline;"> markets.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;">Principles of Consolidation</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">The consolidated financial statements include the accounts of the Company and its wholly-owned subsidiary.&nbsp;&nbsp;All significant inter-company balances and transactions have been eliminated.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;">Fiscal Period</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">The Company uses a 52-53 week fiscal year ending the Saturday nearest </font><font style="display: inline;">to </font><font style="display: inline;">March 31</font><sup style="display: inline;">st</sup><font style="display: inline;">.&nbsp;&nbsp;Fiscal years 20</font><font style="display: inline;">13, 2012 </font><font style="display: inline;">and 20</font><font style="display: inline;">11</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">each </font><font style="display: inline;">comprised 52 weeks. </font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">

The Company also monitors its investments for impairment periodically and records appropriate reductions in carrying values when the declines are determined to be other-than-temporar</font><font style="display: inline;">y.</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">Investments categorized as trading consisted entirely of investments in mutual funds held by the Company&#x2019;s </font><font style="display: inline;">Non-qualified </font><font style="display: inline;">Deferred Compensation Plan (&#x201C;NQDCP&#x201D;) and are included as short-term investments on the consolidated balance sheets.</font>

			<font style="display: inline;">The Company&#x2019;s short-term and long-term investments as of </font><font style="display: inline;">March 30, 2013</font><font style="display: inline;"> are com</font><font style="display: inline;">posed of </font><font style="display: inline;">municipal bonds, corporate bonds, ARS, government agency bonds, </font><font style="display: inline;">commercial papers</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">and</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">certificates of deposits</font><font style="display: inline;">.&nbsp;&nbsp;Unrealized gains and losses are reported in accumulated other comprehensive income (loss), a separate component of shareholders&#x2019; equity, net of any related tax effect. Realized gains and losses and declines in value judged to be other than temporary on available-for-sale securities are included in interest income (expense). There we</font><font style="display: inline;">re no realized losses and declines in value judged to be other than temporary recorded in fiscal years </font><font style="display: inline;">2013, 2012 and 2011</font><font style="display: inline;">.&nbsp;&nbsp;For the purpose of computing realized gains and losses, cost is identified on a specific identification basis. </font><font style="display: inline;">T</font><font style="display: inline;">he ARS investments held by the Company as of </font><font style="display: inline;">March 30, 2013</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">have </font><font style="display: inline;">experienced failed auctions due to sales orders exceeding purchase orders, so the Company&#x2019;s ARS investments are considered illiquid until there is a successful auction for them. As of </font><font style="display: inline;">March 30, 2013</font><font style="display: inline;">, the </font><font style="display: inline;">fair</font><font style="display: inline;"> value </font><font style="display: inline;">of </font><font style="display: inline;">$</font><font style="display: inline;">13,800,000</font><font style="display: inline;"> ARS</font><font style="display: inline;"> was presented in long-term investments.</font><font style="display: inline;"> Due to the lack of availability of observable market quotes on the Company&#x2019;s</font><font style="display: inline;"> investment portfolio of ARS, the fair value was estimated based on a discounted cash flow model and included a discount factor for illiquidity of the ARS market. The assumptions used in the discounted cash flow model include estimates for </font><font style="display: inline;">interest rates, timing and </font><font style="display: inline;">amounts of cash flows, liquidity of the underlying security, expected holding periods and contractual terms of the secur</font><font style="display: inline;">ity. </font>

			<font style="display: inline;font-family:Times New Roman;font-style:italic;">Impairment of Long-lived assets</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">The Company routinely considers whether indicators of impairment of long-lived assets are present.&nbsp;&nbsp;If such indicators are present, the Company determines whether the sum of the estimated undiscounted cash flows attributable to the assets in question is less than their carrying value.&nbsp;&nbsp;If less, the Company recognizes an impairment loss based on the excess of the carrying amount of the assets over their respective fair values.&nbsp;&nbsp;Fair value is determined using various approaches, including discounted future cash flows, independent appraisals or other relevant methods.&nbsp;&nbsp;If the assets determined to be impaired are to be held and used, the Company recognizes an impairment charge to the extent the present value of anticipated net cash flows attributable to the asset are less than the asset's carrying value.&nbsp;&nbsp;The fair value of the asset then becomes the asset's new carrying value, which the Company depreciates or amortizes over the remaining estimated useful life of the asset where appropriate. The Company may incur impairment losses in future periods if factors influencing its estimates change. Historically, the Company has not had an impairment charge on its tangible long-lived assets.</font>

For sales to original equipment manufacturers (&#x201C;OEMs&#x201D;), the Company uses either a binding purchase order or signed agreement as evidence of an arrangement.&nbsp;&nbsp;Sales through distributors are evidenced by binding purchase orders on a transaction-by-transaction basis.&nbsp;&nbsp;Sales to distributors are made primarily under arrangements allowing limited rights of return, limited price protection and limited right of stock rotation on merchandise unsold by the distributors.&nbsp;&nbsp;Because of the uncertainty associated with pricing concessions and possible returns, with the exception of certain products, the Company defers the recognition of such sales and the related costs of sales until distributors have sold the merchandise to their end customers. </font><font style="display: inline;">The Company&#x2019;s distributors provide an inventory balance report at the end of each period, which allows the Company to determine products sold to their </font><font style="display: inline;">end customers.</font>

Some of the NRE contracts include formal customer acceptance provisions.&nbsp;&nbsp;In this case at the end of each period, the Company determines whether customer acceptance has been obtained for the specific milestone.&nbsp;&nbsp;If customer acceptance has not been obtained, the Company defers the recognition of such revenue until customer acceptanc</font><font style="display: inline;">e is obtained.</font>

			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;">Recent Accounting Pronouncements</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">In February 2013, Financial Accounting Standard Board (&#x201C;FASB&#x201D;) issued an amendment regarding net income or other comprehensive income in financial statements.&nbsp;&nbsp;This amendment does not change the current requirements for reporting net income or other comprehensive income in financial statements.&nbsp;&nbsp;However, it requires an entity to provide information about the amounts reclassified out of accumulated other comprehensive income by component. In addition, an entity is required to present, either on the face of the statement where net income is presented or in the notes, significant amounts reclassified out of accumulated other comprehensive income by the respective line items of net income but only if the amount reclassified is required under U.S. GAAP to be reclassified to net income in its entirety in the same reporting period. For other amounts that are not required under U.S. GAAP to be reclassified in their entirety to net income, an entity is required to cross-reference to other disclosures required under U.S. GAAP that provide additional detail about those amounts.&nbsp;&nbsp;This amendment is effective prospectively for reporting periods beginning after December 15, 2012 (the fiscal quarter ending June 29, 2013 </font><font style="display: inline;">for the Company</font><font style="display: inline;">).&nbsp; </font>

			<font style="display: inline;">In June 2011, Financial Accounting Standard Board (&#x201C;FASB&#x201D;) issued new authoritative guidance regarding Presentation of Comprehensive Income.&nbsp;&nbsp;This amendment attempts to improve comparability, consistency, and transparency of financial reporting and to increase the prominence of items reported in other comprehensive income.&nbsp;&nbsp;In order to facilitate convergence with International Financial Reporting Standards (&#x201C;IFRS&#x201D;), FASB has decided to eliminate the option to present components of other comprehensive income as part of the statement of changes in shareholders&#x2019; equity.&nbsp;&nbsp;Also, this amendment requires that all non-owner changes in shareholders&#x2019; equity be presented in a single continuous statement of comprehensive income or in two separate but consecutive statements.&nbsp;&nbsp;This amendment is effective for annual periods beginning after December&nbsp;15, 2011 and interim periods within these years (the fiscal quarter ended June 30, 2012 for the Company) and is applied retrospectively.&nbsp;&nbsp;On October 21, 2011, the FASB proposed a deferral of the requirement to present reclassifications of other comprehensive income on the face of the income statement. Companies would still be required to adopt all other requirements contained in the guidance. The adoption of these amended standards affected the presentation of other comprehensive income, as the Company has elected to present two separate but consecutive statements, but did not have an effect on its financial position or results of operations.</font>

		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">2.</font><font style="display: inline;;font-size:12pt;font-family:Times New Roman;text-indent:0pt;margin-left:0pt;width:36pt">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;"></font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;text-transform:uppercase;">Fair Value</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">The Company measures its cash equivalents, short-term investments and long-term investments at fair value.</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">Fair value is defined as the price that would be received from selling an asset and paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date. When determining the fair value measurements for assets and liabilities required or permitted to be recorded at fair value, the Company considers the principal or most advantageous market in which it would transact and considers assumptions that market participants would use when pricing the asset or liability, such as inherent risk, transfer restrictions, and risk of nonperformance.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">A three-tiered fair value hierarchy is established as basis for considering the above assumptions and </font><font style="display: inline;">determining the </font><font style="display: inline;">inputs used in the valuation methodologies in measuring fair values.&nbsp;&nbsp;The three levels of inputs are defined as follows:</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Level 1 &#x2013; Unadjusted quoted market prices for identical assets or liabilities in active markets that the Company has the ability to access.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Level 2 &#x2013; </font><font style="display: inline;">Observable inputs such as q</font><font style="display: inline;">uoted prices for similar assets or liabilities in active markets; quoted prices for identical or similar assets or liabilities in inactive markets.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Level 3 - Valuations based on models where significant inputs are not observable. The unobservable inputs reflect the Company&#x2019;s own assumptions about the assumptions that market participants would use.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">The Company maximizes the use of observable inputs and minimizes the use of unobservable inputs. If a financial instrument uses input that is significant to the fair value calculation, the instrument will be categorized based upon the lowest level of input that is significant to the fair value calculation.&nbsp;&nbsp;The Company&#x2019;s financial assets and liabilities measured at fair value on a recurring basis include cash equivalents and investment securities, both short-term and long-term.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">The carrying value of cash and cash equivalents, accounts receivable, accounts payable and accrued liabilities approximate their fair value due to their short maturities.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">The Company&#x2019;s money market investments, certificates of deposit purchased directly from the bank, and Non Qualified Deferred Compensation (NQDCP) assets and liabilities are valued using Level 1 inputs. Fixed income </font>
		</p>
		<p><font size="1"> </font></p><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:0pt;text-align:center;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">

The valuation of the Company&#x2019;s investment portfolio is subject to uncertainties that are difficult to predict. The significant unobservable inputs for ARS are illiquidity, term and coupon forecast assumptions. The illiquidity</font><font style="display: inline;"> and term</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">assumptions</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">are</font><font style="display: inline;"> negatively correlated to the fair value. An increase</font><font style="display: inline;">/</font><font style="display: inline;">decrease in the determined illiquidity</font><font style="display: inline;"> or term</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">assumption </font><font style="display: inline;">will lower</font><font style="display: inline;">/</font><font style="display: inline;">increase the fair value. The coupon forecast is positively correlated to the fair value. An increase</font><font style="display: inline;">/</font><font style="display: inline;">decrease in the determined coupon forecast will increase</font><font style="display: inline;">/</font><font style="display: inline;">decrease the fair value. A permutation that includes a change in the coupon forecast with a change in either or both of the two variables will mitigate the significance of the change to the fair value. </font>

During the fiscal years ended March 31, 2012 and April 2, 2011, the Company disposed of short-term available-for-sale securities totaling $</font><font style="display: inline;">166,681,000</font><font style="display: inline;"> and $</font><font style="display: inline;">142,098,000</font><font style="display: inline;">, respectively.&nbsp;&nbsp;The realized gains and losses of these transactions were immaterial. </font>

			<font style="display: inline;">Historically, given the liquidity created by auctions, the Company&#x2019;s ARS were presented as current assets under short-term investments on the Company&#x2019;s balance sheet. However, since the fourth quarter of fiscal 2008 the ARS held by the Company have experienced failed auctions due to sales orders exceeding purchase orders, so the Company&#x2019;s ARS are considered illiquid until there is a successful auction for them.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Accordingly, ARS with a par value of $</font><font style="display: inline;">15,050,000</font><font style="display: inline;"> and $</font><font style="display: inline;">28,050,000</font><font style="display: inline;"> were classified as non-current assets and were presented in long-term investments at fair value of $</font><font style="display: inline;">13,800,000</font><font style="display: inline;"> and $</font><font style="display: inline;">25,900,000</font><font style="display: inline;">, respectively, as of March 30, 2013 and March 31, 2012.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">The ARS are investments with contractual maturities generally between </font><font style="display: inline;">24</font><font style="display: inline;"> to </font><font style="display: inline;">28</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;years. They are in the form of auction rate bonds, whose interest rates had historically been reset every </font><font style="display: inline;">seven</font><font style="display: inline;"> to </font><font style="display: inline;">thirty-five</font><font style="display: inline;"> days through an auction process. At the end of each reset period, investors could sell or continue to hold the securities at par. These ARS held by the Company are primarily backed by pools of student loans and a significant portion are collateralized and guaranteed by the United States Department of Education.&nbsp;&nbsp;Until </font><font style="display: inline;">February 2012</font><font style="display: inline;">, the </font><font style="display: inline;">Company's </font><font style="display: inline;">ARS were rated by the major independent rating agencies as AAA.&nbsp;&nbsp;However, one of the securities was downgraded by S&amp;P in February 2012 to AA+</font><font style="display: inline;">, then</font><font style="display: inline;"> in June 2012 to A with a negative outlook </font><font style="display: inline;">and was downgraded </font><font style="display: inline;">by Fitch</font><font style="display: inline;"> in May 2013 to A with a watch negative</font><font style="display: inline;">. &nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">Also in May 2013, the other ARS was downgraded from AAA to AAA with a watch negative</font><font style="display: inline;"> by Fitch. </font><font style="display: inline;">The Company believes th</font><font style="display: inline;">e</font><font style="display: inline;">s</font><font style="display: inline;">e</font><font style="display: inline;"> downgrade</font><font style="display: inline;">s</font><font style="display: inline;"> ha</font><font style="display: inline;">ve</font><font style="display: inline;"> no impact on the fair value of this ARS.</font>
		</p>

		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">On January 2, 2013, the President signed into law The American Taxpayer Relief Act of 2012 (the "2012 Act"). Under prior law, a tax payer was entitled to a research tax credit for qualifying amounts paid or incurred on or before December 31, 2011. The 2012 Act extends the research credit for two years to December 31, 2013. The extension of the research credit is retroactive and includes amounts paid or incurred after December 31, 2011. As a result of the retroactive extension, the Company recognized a tax benefit of approximately $</font><font style="display: inline;">100,000</font><font style="display: inline;">. The tax benefit was recognized in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2013.</font>

		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Deferred income taxes reflect the net effects of temporary differences between the carrying amounts of assets and liabilities for financial reporting purposes and the amounts used for income tax purposes. Management has concluded it is more likely than not that the Company will realize the benefit of its </font><font style="display: inline;">net </font><font style="display: inline;">deferred tax assets. Management reached this conclusion based on its current expectations of future income. Therefore, the amount of the deferred tax asset that is realizable could be reduced in the near term if actual results differ significantly from estimates of future taxable income.</font>

			<font style="display: inline;">I</font><font style="display: inline;">n January 2011</font><font style="display: inline;">, t</font><font style="display: inline;">he Board of Directors </font><font style="display: inline;">designated $</font><font style="display: inline;">60,000,000</font><font style="display: inline;"> of the Company&#x2019;s cash, </font><font style="display: inline;">cash equivalents and investments for a major stock repurchase </font><font style="display: inline;">through March 30, 2013, and </font><font style="display: inline;">accordingly</font><font style="display: inline;"> increased the Company&#x2019;s</font><font style="display: inline;"> share repurchase </font><font style="display: inline;">program</font><font style="display: inline;"> from approximately </font><font style="display: inline;">556,000</font><font style="display: inline;"> shares to </font><font style="display: inline;">2,500,000</font><font style="display: inline;"> shares. The amended repurchase program has no expiration date except</font><font style="display: inline;">,</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">unless extended,</font><font style="display: inline;"> when an aggregate of 2,500,000 shares have been repurchased, either on the open market or through private transactions.</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">From January 2011 through March 30, 2013, the Company applied approximately $</font><font style="display: inline;">32</font><font style="display: inline;"> million to stock repurchases.&nbsp; </font><font style="display: inline;">As of March 30, 2013, there were approximately </font><font style="display: inline;">828,000</font><font style="display: inline;"> shares authorized for future repurchase under the Company&#x2019;s current program.</font>

			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;">Savings and Retirement Plan -</font><font style="display: inline;"> The Supertex 401K Savings and Retirement Plan allows for employee savings intended to qualify under the provisions of Section 401 of the Internal Revenue Code (IRC).&nbsp;&nbsp;Employees having at least three months of service may make pretax contributions of up to the IRC maximum allowable amount of their qualified compensation.&nbsp;&nbsp;The Company matches certain percentages of employee contributions, all of which are </font><font style="display: inline;">100</font><font style="display: inline;">% vested.&nbsp;&nbsp;In fiscal years </font><font style="display: inline;">2013, 2012 and 2011</font><font style="display: inline;">, the Company's matching contributions were </font><font style="display: inline;">$</font><font style="display: inline;">158,000</font><font style="display: inline;">,</font><font style="display: inline;"> &nbsp;$</font><font style="display: inline;">182,000</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">and $</font><font style="display: inline;">179,000</font><font style="display: inline;">, respectively</font><font style="display: inline;">.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;font-style:italic;">Deferred Compensation Plan - </font><font style="display: inline;">The </font><font style="display: inline;">Non-Qualified </font><font style="display: inline;">Deferred Compensation Plan (the &#x201C;NQDCP&#x201D;) is a plan that covers a select group of senior management or highly compensated employees of the Company.&nbsp;&nbsp;The NQDCP was adopted by the Company, effective January 1, 1996.&nbsp;&nbsp;The Plan assets as of </font><font style="display: inline;">March 30, 2013</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">of $</font><font style="display: inline;">9,673,000</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">were</font><font style="display: inline;"> included in short-term investments in the Company's consolidated balance sheet and classified as trading securities.&nbsp;&nbsp;Such assets shall at all times be subject to claims of the general creditors of the Company. The Company&#x2019;s liability for this plan as of March 30, 2013 amounts to $</font><font style="display: inline;">9,673,000</font><font style="display: inline;"> and this amount is included in accrued salaries and employee benefits in the Company&#x2019;s consolidated balance sheet. The Company does not make matching or other contributions to the Plan. An increase or decrease in the fair value of </font><font style="display: inline;">the Company's NQDCP</font><font style="display: inline;"> assets corres</font><font style="display: inline;">ponds to an increase or decrease in the </font><font style="display: inline;">NQDCP</font><font style="display: inline;"> liability. To recognize the increase or decrease in the </font><font style="display: inline;">NQDCP</font><font style="display: inline;"> plan assets, </font><font style="display: inline;">we</font><font style="display: inline;"> record the difference in fair value to other income (expense) net. Correspondingly, to recognize the increase or decrease in the </font><font style="display: inline;">NQDCP</font><font style="display: inline;"> liability, </font><font style="display: inline;">we</font><font style="display: inline;"> record the difference to other benefits expense.</font>

Under the 2009 Plan, the total number of shares of </font><font style="display: inline;">Company</font><font style="display: inline;"> common stock reserved for issuance&nbsp;&nbsp;consists of </font><font style="display: inline;">1,000,000</font><font style="display: inline;"> shares plus (1) the </font><font style="display: inline;">159,509</font><font style="display: inline;"> shares which remain</font><font style="display: inline;">ed</font><font style="display: inline;"> authorized for issuance under the 2001 Plan but which were not subject to outstanding stock awards as of August 14, 2009, and (2) </font><font style="display: inline;">those of </font><font style="display: inline;">the </font><font style="display: inline;">1,440,400</font><font style="display: inline;"> shares subject to stock awards outstanding under the 2001 Plan as of August 14, 2009, that terminate prior to exercise and would otherwise be returned to the share reserves under the 2001 Plan, with the total shares in addition to the 1,000,000 shares </font><font style="display: inline;">thus </font><font style="display: inline;">being up to a maximum of </font><font style="display: inline;">1,599,909</font><font style="display: inline;"> shares. The 2009 Plan allows the Company to continue its prior option practices under the 2001 Plan to grant non-statutory options to key employees with an exercise price equal to the fair market value of the Company&#x2019;s stock on the date of grant. The Company&#x2019;s options typically have a term of </font><font style="display: inline;">ten</font><font style="display: inline;"> years and vest over </font><font style="display: inline;">five</font><font style="display: inline;"> years, </font><font style="display: inline;">20</font><font style="display: inline;">% on the date </font><font style="display: inline;">one</font><font style="display: inline;"> year after their vesting start date and </font><font style="display: inline;">20</font><font style="display: inline;">% at the end of each of the following </font><font style="display: inline;">four</font><font style="display: inline;"> years. The 2009 Plan also provides the Company with the flexibility in designing equity incentives, including restricted stock awards, stock appreciation rights, restricted stock unit awards, performance stock awards, and performance cash awards. </font>

			<font style="display: inline;">During the fiscal year ended </font><font style="display: inline;">March 30, 2013</font><font style="display: inline;">, the Company granted </font><font style="display: inline;">87,500</font><font style="display: inline;"> options with an estimated total grant date fair value of $</font><font style="display: inline;">698,000</font><font style="display: inline;"> to its employees</font><font style="display: inline;">. During the fiscal year ended March 31</font><font style="display: inline;">, 2012</font><font style="display: inline;">, the Company granted </font><font style="display: inline;">374,580</font><font style="display: inline;"> options with an estimated total grant date fair value of $</font><font style="display: inline;">2,951,000</font><font style="display: inline;">.&nbsp;During the fiscal year ended </font><font style="display: inline;">April 2, 2011</font><font style="display: inline;">, the Company granted</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">285,040</font><font style="display: inline;"> options with an estimated total grant date fair value of $</font><font style="display: inline;">2,891,000</font><font style="display: inline;">.</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">As of </font><font style="display: inline;">March 30, 2013</font><font style="display: inline;">, the unrecognized employee stock-based compensation cost balance related to stock options, net of forfeitures</font><font style="display: inline;">, &nbsp;</font><font style="display: inline;">was </font><font style="display: inline;">$</font><font style="display: inline;">3,531,000</font><font style="display: inline;"> and will be recognized over an estimated weighted average amortization period of approximately </font><font style="display: inline;">1.72</font><font style="display: inline;"> years.</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="font-style:italic;display: inline;font-weight:bold;">Valuation Assumptions </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">In valuing the stock-based compensation expense, the options and awards were stratified into two categories, namely: directors and officers (&#x201C;D&amp;O&#x201D;) and all other employees (&#x201C;All Others&#x201D;), as the experiences of these two groups were different for the expected term of the options. The fair value of each option grant is estimated on the </font><font style="display: inline;">date of grant using the Black-Scholes option valuation model using the following assumptions:</font><font style="display: inline;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<div style="width:100%"><table cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0" style="border-collapse:collapse;width: 100.00%;margin-left:0pt;">
			<tr>
				<td valign="bottom" style="width:28.12%;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-left:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-right:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;background-color: #auto;height:1pt;padding:0pt;">
					<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 0.05pt;font-family:Times New Roman;height:1pt;overflow:hidden;font-size: 1pt">
						<font style="display: inline;font-size:1pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
				</td>
				<td valign="bottom" style="width:02.36%;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-left:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-right:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;background-color: #auto;height:1pt;padding:0pt;">
					<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 0.05pt;font-family:Times New Roman;height:1pt;overflow:hidden;font-size: 11pt">

			<font style="display: inline;">The Company analyzed various data points to determine the most accurate expected term by group. In the course of its analysis, it considered various factors, including vesting terms and period of awards, contractual term of the award, employee historical exercise, post-vesting employment termination behavior, expected term data from peer companies and various other factors.&nbsp;&nbsp;The Company has identified its own historical volatility to be the most appropriate and most representative of the expected volatility rate to be used for valuing stock-based compensation under the Black-Scholes option-pricing model. The expected volatility was based on the expected term of the two groups of options to be valued.&nbsp;&nbsp;The Company continues to use the estimate of risk-free rate based on the U.S. Treasury yield curve in effect at the time of grant.&nbsp; </font><font style="display: inline;">The Company since inception has never paid a regular dividend, only paying a special dividend during fiscal 2013 of $1.00 per share of outstanding common stock, totaling $11,523,000. As a result, the Company assumes an expected dividend yield of zero</font>

		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Arial;;font-size: 11pt"><font style="display: inline;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size:11pt;">12.&nbsp;&nbsp;NET INCOME PER SHARE</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 5pt;font-family:Times New Roman;font-size: 11pt">
			<font style="display: inline;">Basic net income per share is calculated in accordance with the authoritative guidance for earnings per share, which requires dual presentation of basic and diluted net income per share on the face of the income statement.&nbsp;&nbsp;Basic net income per share is computed as net income divided by the weighted average number of common shares outstanding for the period.&nbsp;&nbsp;Diluted net income per share is computed using the weighted-average number of shares of common stock outstanding plus the effect of all dilutive stock option grants and ESPP shares representing potential shares of common stock outstanding during the period.</font>
